Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 15th day of November, 1935, between His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada and the government of the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short space of time that remains at my disposal I shall make only a few remarks. It is perhaps too early to pass any considered judgment with regard to the enlarged trade with the United States that will follow as a result of our trade agreement with that country, but already there are some indications of what is likely to take place; for we have the trade figures for January of this year and we can compare them with the trade figures for January, 1935. Our exports to the United States for January, 1935, amounted to $17,872,669, wrhereas our exports for January, 1936, amounted to $20,872,966, an increase of approximately 17 per cent. On the other hand our imports from the United States for January, 1935, amounted to $23,156,701 whereas our imports for January, 1936, amounted to $26,284,935, an increase of approximately 13^ per cent.
Some of the commodities exported to the United States are striking; I shall deal with one of them. Our exports of cattle, for example, increased from $67,647 in January, 1935, to $498,270 in January, 1936. Our exports of shingles doubled; our exports of planks, boards and other kinds of lumber also showed substantial increases.
The speech delivered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was a remarkable address; it made a number of things perfectly clear to this house and to the people of Canada. In the first place-I think it cannot be disputed-the speech of the right hon. gentleman made it perfectly clear to everyone in Canada that if the Conservative party had been returned to office Canada would not have had any trade agreement with the United States at the present time. The right hon. gentleman blames the government for not obtaining greater concessions from the United States, and then in the next breath he says that he would not give the United States the concessions they ask, at any price. How can trade with any country be built up with that attitude of mind towards it? The right hon. gentleman wants everything his own way; that is not conducive to the building up of trade with other countries. He is very much like the spoiled boy who will not play with the boy next door unless he can have the play all his own way.
Then the speech delivered by the right hon. leader of the opposition showed a peculiar attitude towards trade agreements that is not conducive to international good will. He showed much the same attitude during the negotiation of the Ottawa agreements. He desired to give Great Britain a preference in Canada, but before doing so he raised the tariff sky high so that what seemed to be a preference to Great Britain was in reality no preference at all. Now the right hon. gentleman wants to know what we intend to do with regard t-o the intermediate tariff. Why should he be concerned with what our attitude is going to be during this session towards the intermediate tariff? Would that affect his attitude towards this agreement? Would he vote for this agreement if he were told that immediately after that we would increase the intermediate tariff? Would he have the government do that; would he have this parliament pass this trade agreement and then, immediately after passing it, during this very same session, raise the intermediate tariff? Is that the spirit that should be shown in bringing about a trade agreement? Is that what he is asking us to do? In effect that would be a breach of the spirit, at any rate, of the trade agreement which we are now considering.
The speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition shows very distinctly the fundamental difference that exists between the party of which he is the leader and the Liberal party with regard to tariff and trade matters. We on this side of the house desire an enlargement of our trade with other countries. We are willing to make concessions to other countries in return for a fair and reasonable prospect of enlarging our trade with them. We are satisfied with a fair exchange, and we believe that in this trade agreement we are making a fair exchange with the United States. But there is another difference between the viewpoint of the Conservative party and the viewpoint of those who sit on this side of the house. Personally I do not like the word "concession " as applied to the tariff reductions that we have made. We are not making these tariff reductions in any sense as concessions to the United State? We do not regard

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
them as gifts to the United States; we regard them as tariff reductions made in pursuance of the Liberal policy with regard to the tariff. We wish to make substantial tariff reductions in Canada for the benefit of the Canadian people, regardless of whether we get concessions from other countries or not. If we can get concessions, well and good, but whether we get concessions or not we on this side of the house feel that the time has come when substantial reductions should be made in our own tariff. The Liberal party was elected on a platform of substantial tariff reductions. The tariff structure in this country is much too high. We have had five years' experience of high tariff policy, and I think it has been demonstrated throughout the whole of Canada that that policy has failed. There are many commodities on which in the interests of the producers and the consumers of Canada we require an immediate and substantial decrease in the tariff.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman's time has expired.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I have only a word or
two more. We wish substantial reductions on such commodities as gasoline, agricultural implements and textiles, to mention only a few. This country has suffered from the policy of high tariffs, not merely in one section but in all sections. The overwhelming vote given to the Liberal party meant that Canada did not wish to endure any longer a policy such as that from which it suffered during the preceding five years. Substantial tariff reductions are demanded, and it is the duty of the Liberal party to carry out the mandate given to it by the people of Canada.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take advantage of this my first opportunity to congratulate you on your elevation to your high office, and in the same sentence may I add my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker.
I hope my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Thorson) does not go away, because I am going to have something to say to him in a few minutes; meantime I would much rather address myself to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who consummated this Canada-United States trade agreement. During the past twenty-five years it has been my experience to have pass over my desk from week to week invoices for one or two cars of goods going out of this country and one or two coming into Canada, so that by absorption if in no other way I should have some idea what it means to trade with

our American cousins. Perhaps that is why I was interested enough to sit quietly and listen to the Prime Minister expound to us what I hoped would be shown to be the benefits of this trade agreement to our Canadian people. I listened to a long historical review of what had been done in the past, and what they had tried to do with regard to negotiating a treaty. When he came to something political that might sound good to the ears of his followers he stressed it very heavily, but to my idea this agreement is entirely bereft of any virtue or good result in the main to our Canadian people. I was thinking of those Canadians who to-day are on the relief roll, and those good Canadians who find their vocation in industry. I heard that the Prime Minister went across the street in Ottawa to the United States representative and asked for an interview with the president of the United States, because he was going south for a holiday. A Florida frolic! I thought one of his proteges from Ontario did enough of that during the last two years, according to the press reports, to prevent the Prime Minister giving to the press a statement that he was going south for a Florida frolic. However the interview was arranged; the Prime Minister went to Washington, called on the Canadian legation and stayed overnight in the White House-all the things which he said had been done previously by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). He achieved the interview with the president, as the leader of the opposition did, slept overnight in the White House in like manner, I suppose had the same brand of orange juice for his breakfast in the morning, and I suppose slept in the same bed. At any rate the next morning he gave a statement to the press. Then instead of going south for his Florida frolic he hastened back because Armistice day was approaching, and he made a statement in Canada. I hope there was no political significance attached to that; I do not think there was. However, it will be said that he did a great deal more than the leader of the opposition; he consummated an agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I admit at once-the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) says "hear, hear"-that he did consummate an agreement. And it will be said that it was on the same basis as the leader of the opposition was negotiating an agreement previously. That side of the picture is perhaps true, but the leader of the opposition stopped and waited to see whether we were going to get everything which which it was in the power of the president to give, inasmuch as the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Prime Minister gave everything which it was in his power at that time to give. He gave most favoured nation treatment; he gave the intermediate tariff-I ask my hon. friends not to go too far away; I shall have something more to say about the intermediate tariff. When he gave this intermediate tariff of course he left a loophole so that when the budget comes down my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, one of those orthodox Liberals that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Mallette) was talking about the other evening, along with his orthodox cabinet, can deal with it. And he will get the support of a lot of other people if he does see to it that when it comes to arranging the intermediate items in our tariff the livelihood of those of our citizens who find themselves in difficult circumstances trying to continue to produce in industry will have an opportunity to live. I would like, Mr. Speaker, to have your position for about a week. If I had it I would make a gangway just beyond these ultra-Conservatives like the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) down there so that the radical breezes from the southeast corner would not blow over here and contaminate us. I would take these radical Liberals, these enthusiasts that come from Rosthern or some such place, even my hon. friend from Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), make room for them down beyond the gangway, and pick out a seat for the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), because he will want to sit beyond that gangway by the time the orthodox Liberals are separated from the radicals that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier was telling us about not long ago. I ask you, sir, is it fair to expect us to vote on the Canada-United States trade agreement when we do not know what is going to happen when the budget comes down? I do not think it is. However, here we have it, a white paper with a list of goods which can now enter the United States a little easier, and a great long list which can now flow into this country a little easier. Look at it any way you like; analyze it, and in the main you will find that the products of our primary producers are going to be able to enter the United States a little easier. Yes, we are thankful for that. In a moment I will deal with cattle. But in the main, as far as goods coming into this country are concerned, they will be manufactured and partly manufactured goods. What does that mean? What is going to be the result? It is difficult to prophesy, but we have before us the record of the last twenty-five years, since the 1911 reciprocity
deal was sponsored by my hon. friends opposite. As briefly as I can I shall try to recite its effect. First take the railway situation; the Jersey Central, the Illinois Central, the New York Central, the Chicago, Minneapolis & St. Paul, all those railroads running, like the Mississippi river, north and south, depositing their wares close to the border of Canada; you will find more and more of these manufactured goods coming into Canada, whereas our great railroad systems running east and west will lose the most of their revenue from the long freight haul on the traffic which bears the highest freight rates, that is, manufactured and partly manufactured goods. This agreement will tend to divert that trade north and south; it will not help the east and west trade and therefore will not help our railroad problem. The Chicago, Minneapolis & St. Paul will carry goods into our western provinces; the New England lines will supply the maritime provinces; Detroit and Michigan will be supplying southwestern Ontario; Buffalo and that part of New York state will be supplying the Niagara peninsula and Toronto, and Seattle will be supplying British Columbia. Is that going to help our railway situation? Not as I see it. Time will not permit me to go into more detail, but before passing the subject may I say this: When by the agreement the government did away with the preferential position held by our ports of Saint John, Halifax, Quebec and Vancouver, which enjoyed a ten per cent reduction of the duty payable on goods coming to those ports it made a most unnecessary move. It was not necessary to do that. I say that it was not necessary to put New York, Boston and Seattle in the same position as the other ports I have mentioned. Hon. members opposite say that it was. The railways say that we get millions of dollars of revenue from the haul of export goods from midwestern states through Canada.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Of course we do. and ever shall. My hon. friend pounds his desk. Look at the geography; look at your maps, if you have not looked at them, and trace the shortest route to the seaboard from the great Chicago market. Find the shortest route for the export of goods going to London and Liverpool markets. Those goods come through Canada; the freight will find its way through the shortest possible and least expensive route which, fortunately for us, is through Canada. The alibi of some private member in Albany or a senator in Washington introducing a bill is all humbug and eye-wash, to my idea,

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
because business will find its channel along the lines of smallest cost. That is my experience and it has been the experience of other business men, regardless of the sentimental idea that our United States cousins would force these goods to go over their own railroads. I would remind the house that their railways run north and south, anyway.
I do not know the constituency of my hon. friend, but he seems to be taking an active interest in the subject. I may have something to say to him in a moment or two.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: My interest is in the new senator who has just entered the gallery.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I will leave it to the maritime righters to rise in their places and tell us all about the port preference. Perhaps they may be moved down beyond the gangway, before the next four years are over.
I shall return to a discussion of the remarks of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson), and shall deal with his observations on the Ottawa trade agreements. I wonder if he has been in a huddle with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) in his consideration of this matter. I wonder if he has looked at the figures; I wonder if he has looked at the statistics; I wonder if he really thinks they are as iniquitous as he would have us believe. I wonder if when he was speaking about the increase of trade with the United States in January he would not have been more fair if he had shown that whereas there was an increase of $5,600,000 in exports to the United States in that month, at the same time we had an increase of $6,000,000 to the United Kingdom, due to the Ottawa trade agreement. Why did he not put all the figures and all the facts on record, if he wanted to put any of them before the house.
He has said that the tariff was raised two hundred per cent, but he does not mean that. He has stated that an unfriendly spirit has been engendered in Great Britain towards Canada, but he knows that is not true. He knows that when a question was asked in the House of Commons on December 10 of last year by Sir Percy Hurd I think it was, the reply by the Right Hon. D. Hacking, Under Secretary of State, was in most friendly terms. The hon. member for Selkirk quoted nothing to support his statement, but I shall give something to support mine.
Looking over my files I find a letter dated February 3, addressed to me from Kingsway, England. This letter contains a review of general conditions. There is one page dealing with Russia, another with Germany, another with Prance, and then some observations on this country. My English correspondent is a

director of organizations employing at least
3,000	people; he is connected with seventeen concerns, is chairman of a European cartel and knows whereof he speaks. He says:
In this country-
The United Kingdom.
-our position following Ottawa and the duties which were imposed here, is distinctly improved. Production has increased and we have gained a larger share of our home trade which has benefited us in spite of the fact that prices have shown a tendency to fall rather than to increase as a result of the tariff.
We have made substantial strides in general production as well as in special production, and are now getting a very substantial share of the home trade in the former category as well as in the latter. One result of the tariff has been that this country is taking its proper place as an important producer.
I have given a statement supported by evidence, whereas my bon. friend's iniquitous statement was one without any evidence of fact behind it. To substantiate the facts I shall quote figures supplied by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. These figures show that our domestic exports to the United Kingdom increased from $16,611,036 in January, 1935, to $21,682,840 in January, 1936. At the same time I admit there was only a small increase in our imports from the United Kingdom. Then, we find a substantial increase in yearly exports to the United Kingdom, and we find that they jumped from $174,043,725 in 1932 to $184,361,019 in 1933, $227,601,411 in 1934 and $274,182,737 in 1935. I ask the hon. member to go home and ask some of the hog producers of the dominion how they fee'l about the empire trade treaty. They saw the production of 6,000,000 hogs per annum raised from the four dollar per hundred price level which was prevailing. One year it is raised to six dollars, then the next year to eight dollars, at which price it remained, and we have poured $24,000,000 into the pockets of the Canadian farmers in one year and $48,000,000 in the next year by raising that level. I ask the hon. member if that was so iniquitous or if it was hard for us to take. Was it hard on the Canadian people? Did it make for what he called empire nationalism?
The hon. member has said that the trade agreement with the United Kingdom made it more difficult for us to make agreements elsewhere. He suggested that we were becoming nationalistic and empire minded. I say to the hon. member for Selkirk here and now that this Canada-United States agreement will do more towards Americanizing us than did the United Kingdom agreement towards making us more British. I ask him to take

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
his choice; does he wish to be more Americanized? In twenty-five years does he wish to see this country another state of the union-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
-or would he not be more content to be a little more imperialistic? That is all I have to say to the hon. member for Selkirk.
In the next sentence I admit that there are some good features in the United States agreement.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: The Minister of Finance does not seem to think that that is sensible or logical.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: I do; it is the first logical thing the hon. member has said.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Let me make this general observation. Had we remained in the same position we were in in 1911, then if we had passed the 1911 treaty and had no increase in the export of raw materials and no increase in the importation of manufactured goods it would mean that because of the treaty $58,000,000 less would be paid out through the payrolls in Canada than was the case last year. I prophesy this, Mr. Speaker, that if the government goes the way the radical Liberals want them to go, not the orthodox chaps, that is what is going to happen, and instead of having a balanced economic life as we have in Canada to-day, we will have an economic life very much out of balance; our people would have to revert to primary industry when everybody knows in his heart that that is the last thing they will do. Let me illustrate that trend. People are prone to say to-day that machinery is displacing labour, and to a degree it certainly is, but primary production in this country to-day is nevertheless employing the same number of people that it did in 1910 whereas manufacturing industry has jumped from
400,000	to 600.000.
In 1910 two-thirds of our people were engaged in primary production and one-third were engaged in secondary production, but to-day fifty per cent of our people are in one category and fifty per cent in the other. If you leave out the people engaged in services [DOT]-I refer to people such as are members of this assembly, non-producers, educationalists, men who look after our spiritual welfare, doctors and all those others who look after our services-if you take out that one million and leave only the producers, primary and secondary, you have the balanced national life such as we have in Canada to-day. And that proves my point, which is that there has been retained for Canada an annual payroll of $60,000,000 by the rejection of the 1911 treaty. So I say to you orthodox Liberals, if you accept this Canada-United States agreement you will jeopardize the future of this country to the extent I have indicated, and I do not think you want to do that. In other words, Mr. Speaker, get the gangway ready and let us find out who is who on this agreement.
I would not say anything to my hon. friend from Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston) if he were not a former member of this house. But last night he rose in his place and deprecated the increasing costs of agricultural implements. Agricultural production has gone down and manufacturing production has gone up, and so we have a more balanced economic life in this country. Our production of products of agriculture, forests, fisheries, mining and electric power amounts to $1,051,543,238, or a

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
rate is 27| per cent. The furniture industry-employs 7,783 men and 565 women and pays wages and salaries amounting to $7,000,000. There are 380 factories in Canada and the industry as a whole has had very difficult times. During the past five years business has shrunk twenty, thirty and forty per cent. Furniture can be produced much more cheaply in the southern States than in Canada. The cost per unit is much less because of the greater use of automatic machinery to displace labour. The factories in Grand Rapids, Michigan, are more than anxious to supply western Canada with the necessary furniture. These manufacturers know and the government knows that this Canadian industry has had its trials and troubles because of the industrial codes which have been put upon the statute books of the province of Ontario. These employers are finding it difficult to get along and the government should be fair to them and give them an opportunity to survive.
I notice that it is intended to permit a tourist to bring back $100 worth of goods every time he goes to New York. The other Sunday evening a lady and her daughter came to my house for dinner. She told me that she had been in New York the week before with her daughter and that they had both bought new ensembles. They intended to go down to the Sunnyside boardwalk on Easter morning if it was fine and display their two hundred dollar purchases. Each and every year from 500,000 to 1,000,000 people cross the border between this country and the United States. I am not one who believes that because there are twelve times as many people south of the line, we can expect twelve times as much trade. If these million people who go back and forth every year bring in only one-half their quota of goods, it means goods to the value of $50,000,000. When this amount is broken down, as I indicated a few moments ago with other figures, it represents a reduction in the payrolls of Canadian people of $12,500,000 per year. The reduction will be at least that much, if not more.
When people from south of the border come over here they just shoot a few deer and take home the horns. They may take home a box of fish or a few pieces of woollen goods, but that is all. When it comes down to the question of style, we go to the United States. Look at what the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) brought from Broadway? What do you think of that? Was that made in New York? Goods brought home from New York! See the cut of it!

But in garments such as these, in which my hon. friends may strut around, will be twenty-five dollars' worth of wages for an American citizen, wages taken from a Canadian. And what applies in that regard will apply not only to dress goods, but to Edison inventions of one kind or another, Westing-house inventions of one kind or another, parts of this, that and the other, all the handicrafts of Americans who set the style, who set the vogue, who give us our new inventions, let in to the tune of $50,000,000, twelve and a half million dollars of which is taken from the wage earners of Canada.
While the present Prime Minister was in power for the ten years from 1921 to 1931,
11255,000	of our people left Canada and 288,000 Canadians returned to Canada-a loss of close to a million in ten years; 100,000 a year on the average went south. They are not going south now; they are coming back. The duty of the Prime Minister as I see it is to provide for them, to provide for the employables, to provide for those who are to-day engaged in industry, and to see to it that his broad ideals about free trade and breaking dawn the barriers of world tariffs here and there do not blind him to his responsibility first to tackle the problem of finding work for the minds and hands of all kinds and classes of our people to-day, and then to go carefully on agreements such as this.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	Mr. Speaker, as I listened to
the organ tones of my hon. friend from Dan-forth (Mr. Harris) I could realize the joy that is in his heart because at last he is able to get up once more and make a typical old-fashioned, 1911, Tory, no truck or trade with the Yankees speech. I know how much he enjoys doing that, and we should allow him a little latitude because, during the months immediately prior to October 14 last, think of the repression which my hon. friend from Danforth had to exercise while his leader and other leaders of his party were making pilgrimages to Washington, almost on their hands and knees, in an endeavour to secure from that country an agreement which could not do for this country what the agreement of 1911 would have done had it been executed.
This government entered into the agreement with the United States of America because we sincerely believe that agreement to be a good thing for the Canadian people. We also believe that it is a good thing for the American people. We do not view matters of trade as matters of war, but we do view trade as a means of building up

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
mutual interests. We believe it to be possible on the basis of the start now made, a start which has been striven for by people of good will in both countries for many years, to go forward and develop to the mutual advantage of people on both sides of the international border an ever increasing volume of trade. We do not claim perfection for the treaty. The negotiation of it was necessarily surrounded by the limitations which were upon the governments of both countries, limitations which have been discussed by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). This much is clear, however, from our point of view, that when the right hon. leader of the opposition says that he refused to sacrifice his country, thereby implying that we have done so, we make no great professions of pluperfect patriotism; we are not entitled to use the words "my country," as he does; we can only use the words "our country." We have not as large a proprietary interest in it, it is true, but we are Canadians, and we resent that old Tory accusation that we are sacrificing our country. No man in this house, no matter what his party, would intentionally sacrifice his country. We may make mistakes in judgment-'all of us, I presume, have done so- but I do not believe there is a man in this house who falls short of another in his affection for and his support of this Dominion of Canada and its people.
With regard to my right hon. friend's speech I want to point out one or two things in it, in the short time at my disposal, and I shall hurry on and adhere very closely to my notes.
The right hon. gentleman indicated percentages of reduction in the treaty on United States goods coming into Canada, and he rolled over his tongue "100 per cent," "50 per cent," and another percentage, but he did not of course tell the house that these percentage reductions were exactly those involved in his note of November 14, 1934, to the government of the United States; that the offer made by my right hon. friend and his government involved all the percentage reductions he referred to.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must rise to a question of order. There was no offer made. There was an offer of a basis for negotiations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I expected my right hon. friend to correct me. It was a basis for negotiations. Whoever heard of any one advancing as a basis of negotiations more than he was prepared to give, or demanding in return less than he was prepared to take? This was the commencement of a deal. The advances a basis of negotiations, to use his own language. He does not mean to tell this house that he asked the United States for less than he was willing to take in opening negotiations. I do not think he would ask us to credit anything of the kind. My right hon. friend says, on page 625:
I am one of those who have always been more or less alarmed and concerned about the favoured nation clauses in our treaties.
Well, sir, as a basis of negotiation, on November 14, 1934, he offered the United States of America full most favoured nation benefits in their relations with Canada. Those benefits must necessarily have been exactly the same then as now. There has been no change in the meantime.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will permit me, he has entirely misapprehended the point. The point was that that was the basis of negotiation, depending entirely upon what we got for it, and unless we got suffi-cent for it we would not give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I shall come to that point presently. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will remember these interruptions. Unlike my right hon. friend, I have not three hours; I have only forty minutes in which to develop my argument.
Then on page 627 my right hon. friend says:
That means that we have bound ourselves not to increase the duties, either intermediate or general, during the term of this agreement on those seventy-seven items.
This is an entire misapprehension of fact. There is no such undertaking anywhere in the agreement as far as the general tariff is concerned. Later on the same page my right hon. friend refers to the right granted the nationals of any country under the intermediate tariff to bring in their goods through other intermediate countries, and he says that the practice of goods passing through other intermediate countries started with the French agreement of 1922. Perhaps the point is not of very great importance, except for the reference made to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in that connection, but I would point out that the same provision was in force for many years prior to 1922 and occurred specifically in the agreement with France negotiated in 1907. In fact it was in existence for many years prior to that in connection with British treaties to which our young dominion adhered. I might specially mention the old arrangement with Switzerland. It will be evident to everyone that it must have been the case in connec-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
tion with any agreement with that country, because Switzerland is entirely an inland country and goods passing from Switzerland to Canada necessarily must pass through another country in order to reach our shores.
Then there is a most astonishing statement by my right hon. friend which apparently he expects us to take for granted. He says:
I need hardly point out that in all the treaties that have been negotiated up to the present-and this we did point out with as much clarity as possible-we proceeded on the assumption that the United States was under the general tariff.
Then he goes on:
I am not in a position at the moment to state what will be the result in the various countries with whom we have treaties, now that they find themselves no longer under their special treaties, meeting the conditions provided thereby, but are faced with a new set of conditions under which the nearby United States of America enjoys the same benefits and in some instances even greater benefits-*
And so on. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is a most astonishing statement, the idea that we told or implied to countries with whom we entered into agreements down through the years that the United States always would be under the general tariff, and that these countries, though they were getting only our intermediate tariff, could always rely on this great potential competitor, the United States, being subject to our general tariff. Well, certain fairly recent negotiations, those of 1932, under the late administration may have been carried on in that spirit or attitude of mind, but surely it was never stated by anyone in authority, even under the extraordinary circumstances of 1932, that the United States would remain always under the general tariff. No more was any such promise, statement or implication given in respect of Canada's past negotiations with any other country, British or foreign.
I am attaching very considerable importance to this, Mr. Speaker, and am being very careful of my words because it is an extraordinary spectacle to see a former prime minister deliberately suggesting to treaty countries that the government of the day in Canada has so acted that they, the treaty countries, find themselves no longer under their special treaties, to use the right hon. gentleman's own words, meeting the conditions provided thereby, but are faced with a new set of conditions. I quote exactly from my right hon. friend's words. Such an idea, I venture to say, sir, would not occur to any of the countries with whom Canada has commercial agreements, since Canada, no less than they, is free at any time to admit to its

most favoured nation circle any nation on earth not formerly within that circle.
If my right hon. friend believes what he says in this regard how did. he feel free to offer to the United States our intermediate tariff or our most favoured nation treatment? Surely he was not deceiving the United States in making that offer. How then, after the event, can he come here and create doubt in the minds of all those countries with whom Canada at present has trade treaties? Then my right hon. friend goes on to say:
We have built up our ports on that assumption ... on the assumption that in all the treaties we made by which we granted favoured nation treatment to various countries of the world, it would be provided that they would ship their goods direct to this country through a lake, river or sea port.
Again I ask, did my right hon. friend inform the United States that the only kind of agreement he was willing to consider with respect to the United States would be one which compelled all goods coming from that country to Canada to enter in that manner? He knows perfectly well that he did not. It would have been an absurdity when, as a matter of fact, the boundaries of these two countries meet over three thousand miles of land. Such a provision inevitably would mean that parts of Canada could not import goods at all from the United States under the provisions of the treaty. If my right hon. friend really means what he says in this regard at least he should have pointed out to the United States in his note of November, 1934, that his offer was limited to goods that would be imported at sea, lake or river ports only. Did he do so? No.
Then the right hon. leader of the opposition asks what will be the effect on our railways. I for one am not apprehensive as to the effect on our railways, but I was apprehensive, as I believe members of the previous government were, of the possibilities inherent in the measures which had been proposed on several occasions in the United States congress by way of retaliation on Canada in this regard. There was, as every man who has occupied a position of ministerial responsibility in recent years knows, a grave danger that the White bill, or one of the other retaliatory measures which have been before congress in recent years, might possibly have become law, and it is not too much to say that both our great railway corporations were very apprehensive of the result of such a retaliatory measure on the part of the United States.
Then I come to the effect on our factories. Men are being released from employment, my right hon. friend says, in some of those branch factories to-day because it is cheaper to pro-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
duce the goods in the central United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have made some inquiries. Some of the very few branch factories from which men are being released are branches of United States concerns which have been in existence in Canada in recent years with extremely high protection, achieved by means of arbitrary valuations, which had no economic justification for existence.
Then the right hon. gentleman developed his argument further and said, "We have a right to know whether the intermediate tariff is to be raised or not, because it changes the agreement." Well, Mr. Speaker, in fact it does precisely the opposite, because the agreement itself reserves to the Dominion of Canada full control over its intermediate tariff, with the exception of those items specifically excepted, which are contained in a schedule separate from all the rest. As to the right of the opposition to know to-day what will be proposed in the budget with regard to the intermediate tariff, it would be just as reasonable to ask what will be in the budget with respect to the intermediate tariff next year or the following year. The right of Canada to deal with its intermediate tariff, with the exceptions I have noted, is specifically and clearly preserved in the agreement. And we propose to deal with the intermediate tariff in accordance with the best judgment of this government and in the interests of the people of Canada. We shall propose to the house from time to time, in successive budgets, such modifications, up or down as the case may be, as we feel we can justify to this parliament as being in the best interests of the people of Canada.
Then my right hon. friend' says, on page 629:
The government may reduce every item, in the tariff except those with respect to which they are bound .to specific duties or free entry, ...
Well, Mr. Speaker, the bound items do not bind the government of 'Canada not to reduce.. They merely bind the government of Canada not to increase during the currency of the agreement. We have perfect freedom to reduce the rates with respect to the 'bound items, and my right hon. friend was quite incorrect in his reference to that matter.
Then there was a dramatic interlude. The right hon. gentleman gave a list of items which must be considered by this government -eggs, oats; he goes on all through the list. Now, these items existed in exactly their present form when the basis of negotiation of November 14, 1934, was offered to the United States. My right hon. friend knew at that time that these rates existed and that if he succeeded in making the treaty he would 12739-46
be faced with the question of how items such as these should be dealt with. And he expected, as this government expected-and as this government accomplished-that the right of this parliament to change its intermediate tariff on such items would be entirely preserved. I presume my right hon. friend knew perfectly well that he could not come to this parliament with any agreement which involved a wholesale surrender of the right of parliament to dead with its intermediate tariff. In that regard we agree with him, and we have preserved the right of parliament to deal with its own tariffs.
Then the leader of the opposition becomes very much concerned. He says, "What more can we give the United States than we have already given them under this agreement? What have we left to negotiate with?" "All is lost," he says, "nothing more can be done." What are the facts? Sir, there are hundreds of items in the Canadian tariff on which the existing rates are relatively high and often prohibitive. There are scores of items on which the intermediate tariff is the same as the general. In my humble opinion we have a great deal with which to bargain with the United States, if we wish to put it that way.
Then my right hon. friend got into a little difficulty with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). At page 634 the Minister of Trade and Commerce asked:
Mr. Euler: Did you ask for fifty per cent?
And the leader of the opposition replied:
Mr. Bennett: The question is not whether we asked for fifty per cent; we said fifty per cent would not be adequate.
Now I am in some difficulty, because a great deal of the information regarding these negotiations which is in the possession of the government is necessarily confidential. Obviously also we do not want to be in the position of cross-examining civil servants, who served the late government and serve ourselves faithfully and well. But I can say this, that there is nothing on record anywhere showing that my right hon. friend ever asked for the full fifty per cent, the full extent of the president's powers, across the whole line of the American tariff. There is on the other hand plenty of evidence that my right hon. friend never had in his mind the possibility of getting a fifty per cent cut on the whole American tariff. What is that evidence? What did he suggest as a basis of negotiation? Now, anyone knowing him would know that he would ask for enough. He would surely ask for the utmost possible by way of concession from the United States. And what did he ask for? He asked that the United States should



Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
reduce its tariff by fifty per cent on a specified number of natural products-not all across the board, as he said the other day-and reduce existing rates on a number of partly or wholly manufactured products of Canada. This was offered as a basis of negotiation. If my right hon. friend ever expected to get a fifty per cent cut right across the board, surely he would have asked for it in his basis of negotiation. Surely he did not expect the President of the United States to say: Why Mr. Bennett, you have not asked for enough!
My time is getting along, and I want to deal now with the point of my right hon. friend's argument that we have given far too much for what we have received. What have we given? Again I refer to my right hon. friend's basis of negotiations of November 14,
1934.	He offered the whole intermediate tariff.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I read this:
The mutual concession of tariff treatment as favourable as that accorded to any other foreign country;-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Read the first part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
These are my right hon. friend's own words:
-this means that Canada would extend to the United' States its intermediate tariff-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE

-involving reductions from the present rates of duty on some some seven hundred items, including both natural and manufactured products, together with a number of further reductions below the intermediate tariff rates through the extension to the United States of concessions made by Canada in trade conventions with foreign countries.
That is what my right hon. friend said. Now he says he did not offer the intermediate tariff to the President of the United States.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat that he did not. If the hon. gentleman desires to read from the note, let him read what is said. That was the basis of negotiation; then follows a statement of what we wanted in return, and the Secretary of State wrote to us saying each item would have to be taken up item by item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Of course. But my right hon. friend in this original basis of negotiation offered the intermediate tariff.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: He did not do that. He offered that only as a basis of negotiation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: And he now desires us to believe that he offered as a basis of negotiation something less than he was willing-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: No, he did not say that either. It depended on what he got.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: It is a truly historic document. The man who wrote it is forever estopped from criticizing the treaty which this government entered into.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing the following resolution:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 15th day of November, 1935, between His Majesty's Government in the Dominion of Canada and' the Government of the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
At the outset I wish to say that I propose to support the resolution and to facilitate the introduction of the necessary legislation, so that in its course through the house, in the commitee of the whole and the various stages the details may be discussed.
It is not my present intention to discuss many of those details. A few I shall touch upon by way of illustration, but I do wish to deal with some of the principles involved in, shall I say, this transaction. May I preface what I wish to say a little later on by observing that one could scarcely call this agreement a treaty of reciprocity, in the old acceptation of that term. Rather it is a trade agreement based upon the modern exigencies of the case and the times. I do not believe there is much to be gained by an analytical examination of the history of the two old parties in Canada with respect to the reciprocity policy. A few days ago we listened to the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and he will pardon me if I suggest that the first two hours of his speech spent upon a well worked out historical record was less interesting than the last half hour which dealt with the treaty. I think the same can be said about other speeches we have heard. The argument back and forth as to whether the Tory party was for reciprocity and the Liberal party more so is not of much avail.
I am going to speak for myself. I have been in the house for, I believe, twenty-five years. Up until a year ago, or thereabouts, I was a member of the Conservative party. I cannot recall that during that time the Conservative party favoured reciprocity with the United States. Certainly I did not. I may have been misguided or misled, but certainly I am not going to pretend to the house that I favoured reciprocity, because I did not. In 1911, my first election campaign, I was elected after a very bitter controversy over reciprocity. On many occasions since I have opposed reciprocity in various forms. I would not be true to myself or to my past record were I to pretend to-day that I was or had been in favour of reciprocity.
In 1932 or thereabouts, however, at a time when I was Minister of Trade and Commerce, I realized that the trade relations between Canada and the United States were not on a very good basis. For many years- and I am not excepting the period between 1922 and 1930 when the right hon. gentleman opposite was in power-we had had, shall I say, certain controversial relations with the United States on these matters.

There was no open governmental controversy, but it was well known that the views of leaders in the United States were strongly against reciprocal arrangements with Canada, and on the other hand there was a good deal of criticism in Canada of the attitude of the United States towards entry of our goods. So I might be justified in saying that there was a degree of controversy.
About 1932, in view of conditions that were developing the world over and the inhibitions against Canadian exports entering other countries, I felt that quotas, import restrictions, the raising of tariffs, what is commonly called a national spirit, which was so prevalent and is still so prevalent throughout the world, placed many obstacles in the way of our trade and in the way of trade generally. I felt it was highly desirable that Canada should study the trade relations between our country and the United States, and with that in mind I instructed the staff under me at the time to proceed to a study of the trade between the two countries, and to prepare in detail the items upon which without injury to ourselves and in all fairness to the United States we might offer some considerations for favourable trade. I find in the agreement many of the items which we reviewed about three years ago. Many of the commodities we had studied then are included both in the note of November 14 and in the treaty. Why, under those circumstances, should I oppose the agreement?
In considering this matter I think we might take a look at the world. If we do that we will note that the great continent of Asia is the scene of threatened conflict-I am not overstating it when I use that word-between the great empire of Japan, and Russia, with China as the bone of contention. Every day in press reports we find announcements of new developments, and relations are very much strained. There is little evidence of peace and good will in Asia. Turning to Europe we find all the older and more powerful nations feverishly arming and eagerly making alliances one with the other when they think such alliances will help them in the defence of their realm-not trade agreements, not commercial understandings with each other, but alliances of defence or offence, as the case may be. Africa is a cockpit, and at the present time a slaughter is taking place in that continent which certainly offers a challenge to the modern idea of humanitarian practice. However on the American continents, both north and south, we have a condition of peace and accord, and nothing threatens the good will of our people. I suggest, therefore, that any gesture

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of good will between important countries on the North American continent is a splendid contribution to the general cause of peace and good will and concord, and while the Prime Minister may have exaggerated to some extent its influence on the rest of the world, one thing is certain in my mind, and that is that we would do well to ensure as far as we possibly can that there Shall be enduring peace and concord in this part of the world. I know of no better way, Mr. Speaker, of bringing about that condition than by settling all outstanding trade and commercial difficulties and differences.
May I read an extract from this famous paper that has been quoted so often, and which I agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) is historic and important. I quote from the reply of Mr. Cordell Hull, Secretary of State for the United States, to the famous note of November 14. The American minister in his reply says:
I believe that a point has now been reached when an exchange of views on this subject with Canada should be undertaken, and I am, therefore, gratified to learn that your government is of the same mind. Whatever the *desirability of the freest possible exchange of natural products, and indeed other products, between the United States and Canada as an ultimate goal, the United States government must in any negotiations undertaken at this time restrict itself to measures authorized by the Trade Agreements Act, 1934.
The point to which I wish to call attention in this quotation is that the agreement is obviously looked upon by the government of the United States, and so declared in this historic document, as a step towards some ultimate goal which would be of a wider character than the present agreement or than that which was outlined' in the note of November 14, 1934. And so, Mr. Speaker, in supporting this resolution and facilitating the passage of this measure we are taking, I believe, a step towards a larger and a more complete ultimate understanding with the United States. If that can be achieved I think it is all to the good.
Let us look for a moment at the agreement. The agreement is, as I have said, a step or a gesture in the right direction. I notice that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day seemed desirous of justifying himself for the action he had taken. I want to say to him that I do not think he needs to do that at all. I think that the result of his action is measurably satisfactory. I shall deal with the agreement in more detail a little later on, but on the whole I think he has every reason to believe that he has made a satisfactory arrangement, 
not wholly satisfactory, but a fairly satisfactory arrangement that does not need any justification.
I would like to pause here to commend the utterance of the Prime Minister when he paid tribute to the permanent officers and officials of the government. In his capacity as Prime Minister I suppose it would not have been proper for him to make mention of any particular names, but I do not feel bound, shall I say, by that same degree of reticence. I should like to pay tribute to Doctor Skelton, head of the external affairs department, and his staff, because I know something of the work they have done in this matter. I should like also to pay tribute to Mr. Wilgress and his staff for the splendid detailed work they have done in this and in many other matters. I should also like to pay tribute to Mr. McKinnon, one of the ablest officials that we have in the government of Canada in tariff matters.	I say from
experience and from intimate contact with these and other officials that no minister could possibly discharge his duties in a matter of this kind without having at his elbow these splendid officials, and Canada can well be proud of its permanent civil service. I do not think it is out of the way once in a while to pay public tribute to these men on an occasion of this kind.
I should also like to refer to the work, because I know something of the task that he had, that was done by Mr. Herridge as the representative of this country in Washington. In this connection and in other matters I think his services to Canada are worthy of note and commendation, and I would say to the Prime Minister that neither he nor any other head of the government will lose in dignity or prestige by acknowledging that others within the ambit of government may have some part to play in the success of negotiations of this kind and in the discharge of these very difficult duties.
The Liberal program has frequently cited external trade as a likely cure for many internal ills. The Prime Minister put it in rather eloquent language the other day when he said, "Depression means absence of trade." Then he reversed it and said, "Trade means the end of depression." I should like just here to sound a note of warning and to say that while I take second place to no one in desiring to promote Canada's external trade, we would be misleading the country were we to leave the impression on the minds of those who are to-day unemployed, our agriculturists and our unemployed workers, that their troubles are ended with the expansion

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of trade. That would be a mistake. By all means let us expand our trade and do everything possible in that direction. It may be a contribution towards the ending of commercial stagnation, but it is not a cure for the problems of agriculture and of labour. It may ameliorate present conditions, but it will not cure them or solve our problems, and I think it would be unwise for us to assume that it W'ould.
Coming to the agreement itself, I would say that the making of a treaty is a difficult matter at any time. You cannot always get things and never give something in return; that is clear. It is absurd to suggest that we can reach out and get all we want and give nothing in return. All we have to do is to read the public press and note the grievous complaints made south of the line regarding this trade agreement as evidence that they feel that some of their interests have been sacrificed, while on this side other interests feel that they have been sacrificed. It is not clever to criticize this treaty simply because individual interests may be affected. I am not disregarding them, and I hope time will permit me to touch on a few before I am through, but you could never make any trade agreement if you had to safeguard the interests of every individual in the country. It simply could not be done. There are bound to be some cases where there appears to be an injury, but what I would suggest is that we wait for a time and see whether these imagined injuries are real.
In the first place I want to say that this treaty is good because the motive and intention behind it are good, and I think it should be supported because the motive and intention are good. There is a spirit of good will in the treaty which ought to be and I am sure is welcomed by both countries.
The next point is the most favoured nation provision, about which there is a great deal of misunderstanding. For many years I was one of those who had a doubt, and I still have it, as to the wisdom of originally adopting the most favoured nation system of trade agreements. We have had this provision in effect in this country for twenty years or more, but it has been accentuated during the last sixteen years. During the last fifteen years the government of the right hon. gentleman opposite and the government of hon. members on this side have made in the neighbourhood of twenty to thirty treaties containing such a provision. I believe there are twenty-seven such treaties now outstanding. Let us examine this provision for a moment. It is comparatively simple, but it is significant. I should like to read one or
two extracts from treaties to indicate the wording of this provision. The treaty with Czechoslovakia contains this clause:
Articles the produce or manufacture of Canada imported into Czechoslovakia and articles the produce or manufacture of Czechoslovakia imported into Canada shall not be subjected to other or higher duties or charges than those paid on the like articles the produce or manufacture of any other foreign country.
The treaty with Finland contains a clause which is somewhat different, and which reads:
Goods produced or manufactured in Finland shall receive in Canada treatment as favourable as that accorded to goods produced or manufactured in any other foreign country so long as goods produced or manufactured in Canada enjoy in Finland the same treatment as is enjoyed by similar goods produced or manufactured in the United Kingdom.
There are some twenty-seven similar treaties, the present one making twenty-eight. What does this provision mean? Suppose we made an agreement to-morrow with Honduras-I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) that if we had a treaty with Honduras we could do business with that country which we cannot do at the present time-containing certain concessions. Those concessions would apply to the goods from all the twenty-eight countries with which we have similar treaties. On the other hand, we would enjoy any favour shown by Honduras to any other country.
There is one feature of this matter which has not been noted or recognized. Up until a matter of two or three years ago the historic policy of the United States was one tariff for all. That country has now adopted the system, which we are following in part, of making special agreements with other countries. Where the United States makes an agreement with a country with which we have an agreement, we will enjoy the same privileges as those given to the United States. I believe there are some seven or eight countries with which the United States has made agreements and with which we have also agreements. The two countries will be placed on the same basis and inasmuch as we export many things which are also exported by the United States, we will have an added advantage in those countries.
The next point to which I should like to refer is the maintenance of the free list. Since the change in policy of the United States we have been threatened with the cancellation of favoured treatment in that market unless we made this agreement. That would have been very serious to us. Let me mention a few items on the free list. Last night the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston)

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
brought up the matter of agricultural implements. One of the arguments advanced for a tariff against goods coming into Canada from the United States is the fact that the population of the United States is 120.000,000 while that of Canada is only 10,000,000. That is a perfectly valid argument, but in the case of agricultural implements we have had free access to that market of 120,000,000 people for many years. The bases for the agricultural implement industry in Canada offer first hand opportunities for large production, yet shortly after the signing of this agreement these manufacturers raised their prices. The resolution introduced by the hon. member proposes that an inquiry should be held. Whether or not an inquiry is held, I say to the Prime Minister that he should bring representatives of the International Harvester Company and the Massey-Harris Company, the two largest manufacturers, to Ottawa, and ask them to show reason why prices have been raised. I do not want to impinge upon the other debate, but this is germane to this subject. For the last five or six years the farmers of this country have experienced a diminution in the prices of their products and in their purchasing power. Then just as prices were recovering, just as they were given an opportunity to buy, these implement companies raised their prices, There may be justification for this raise but it is not discernible to the average man. I think they should be called to Ottawa to show cause for these increased prices.
The next item to which I should like to refer is wood pulp. Do hon. members realize what the maintenance of this item upon the free list means? I have before me figures showing the imports into the United States of various kinds of pulp products, such as newsprint and that sort of thing. The total imports in 1935 were 8146,000,000 in round figures. The imports from Canada in that year were valued at 889,000,000; from Newfoundland, 83,700,000; from Norway, $4,600,000; from Sweden, $28,000,000; from Finland, $8,000,000; from Germany, $5,000,000; from Czechoslovakia $1,000,000, and from France $4,800,000. It will be noted from these figures that by no means do we control that market for these products. At the present time we have an advantage because of propinquity to the market, facilities of manufacture, transportation and so on, but there are present all the elements of successful competition from these various countries unless we can maintain our position on the free list. Let us not forget that this is one of the big items of export from this country and it should be safeguarded by every possible means.

For several years there has been a distinct agitation in the United States for a duty against wood pulp and newsprint in order to encourage the production of these articles from southern pine. Successful experiments have been made in the production of these articles from this wood. Take another item. We have had free access to the American market for shingles, and I well remember that for a period of over a year when I was Minister of Trade and Commerce we were labouring under the greatest anxiety because of the efforts that were being made to stop the importation of shingles into the United States. That is something which is vital to the lumber and the shingle industry of British Columbia, and it is safeguarded and ensured and stabilized by this treaty.
Then, as regards squared timbers, ties, poles and posts, here again is a tremendous business of- a very valuable character for the working men of this country, the settlers and people more or less of the poorer class who cut these poles and make these ties; we have free access to the American market for them; it is safeguarded and ensured in this treaty. It is not enough to say that it was free before, because I know from my own experience that in many of these cases we were threatened with the shutting of these commodities out of the American market, or with an impost that would have affected them had we not made this treaty.
There is also the stabilization of our position with regard to cattle, sawn timber, and some, although not enough, of the fish products; there are some we should like to see added. But again I recall to the minds of hon. members what was said by Mr. Cordell Hull, that this was a step towards what it was ultimately hoped to achieve; and what we do not yet have we can hope later on to secure. But we did stabilize certain classes of fish, and particularly lobsters.
There is also an item regarding leather to which I should like just to make reference. I have cited only a few items. There are many others. These are items of major importance to Canadian trade and to the Canadian workman. It was highly desirable that we should ensure that these should be maintained either on the free list, or at a low rate of duty, such as is the case with the items to which I have referred.
No doubt difficulties will arise. It is inevitable and unavoidable in a treaty of this character, particularly after these long years of controversy, not without bitterness, that difficulties and complaints will arise. But I

Caiiada-U. S. Trade Agreement
would remind the house, and I say in all sincerity-that we are free to amend the intermediate tariff if we wish, although I would warn the government and the house that w7e should not exercise that right carelessly; this should be done with tact and courtesy and with consideration for the other party to the agreement. But where it is shown that an injustice is done, where it can be demonstrated that someone or some industry is injured, the proper course is to take the matter up through the usual diplomatic channels with the authorities of the United States, as the treaty in several articles provides, and make suggestions for adjustments along those lines. Undoubtedly suggestions will come from the other side. I have had something to do with several agreements, and I have never known of one where complaints have not arisen from both sides after it was passed, nor have I known of any agreement where adjustments have not been made after it had been signed and put into effect. We cannot give with one hand and withdraw with the other. We must recognize that there are two parties to a deal of this kind.
I should like to make very brief reference to a few matters which appear to me to give some cause for anxiety. There is the question of the hundred dollars free entry. Persons going to the United States may, on returning, bring in goods freely to the value of one hundred dollars. This has been the case in the United States for many years, and during that time Canada has built up quite a nice trade because of that privilege granted to American citizens who come to this country to buy goods and return to the United States with those goods free up to one hundred dollars worth. I should like to suggest to the minister who has charge, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), that the privilege granted in this agreement should be limited distinctly to private purchases. There are certain specialty dealers, particularly in radios, electrical appliances, and some of the higher priced smaller articles, who might take advantage of this provision. By constantly running backwards and forwards from, say the Niagara peninsula to Buffalo, or Windsor to Detroit, or points on the St. Lawrence to various towns on the other side, it might be possible for dealers of that character to take advantage of this one hundred dollars rule to do an injustice to their competitors in Canada. I do not think there should be much difficulty; at any rate I do not think it is beyond the ability of the Department of National Revenue to devise regulations which will safeguard that provision from abuse. I wonder if those whc complain about this realize the advantage that we have now and have had for many years in selling American tourists gifts to the extent of one hundred dollars per person. We must recognize that.
Then the florists are making some complaints, and there is danger there. It is quite true that some distance south it is quite easy to raise all sorts of flowers from bulbs and other stock and ship them into Canada under this treaty. The government ought to take into account that Canadian florists have paid substantial duties on their bulbs, rose-bushes, and other stock of that calibre and are entitled to some consideration in that respect. The case is somewhat complex. On the one hand you have those in Canada who produce bulbs and base stock asking for protection, and then you have dealers of cut flowers, the finished product, also asking for protection, claiming that they have to pay this duty. I suggest to the government that an effort should be made to see that no real injustice is done to those who are producing florist stock in Canada.
The other day when the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) were before the house, reference was made by some of my hon. friends from British Columbia, to baby chicks. This sounds like a trivial matter, although to British Columbia it is of some importance. But I would remind my friends from that province-and I take second place to none of them in my desire to protect its interests-that British Columbia has received splendid concessions on lumber which have already been of tremendous benefit to them. They have the assurance of free entry for shingles, which is of great importance to them. I would remind them that there are some provinces to which we cannot now ship our baby chicks, and I think that before we complain about the danger of competition from the United States we should get the Minister of Agriculture to unravel the problem of shipping our baby chicks within Canada; when we accomplish that, perhaps we can turn our attention to the other matter.
Perhaps we have slipped up on the question of potatoes. As I understand it, there is a duty on Canadian potatoes going into the United States, while United States potatoes come in here free. We have clarified the matter of seed potatoes, but the other question affecting potatoes is rather serious. I do not doubt that it can be rectified if the matter is carefully examined and placed in its proper light. No objection could be found to raising the intermediate duty here
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

if, after such examination, this was deemed desirable. I suggest it is a matter that should receive study and consideration.
I was rather amused at the reference to the furniture industry, that there -was a danger of our driving the furniture manufacturers of Canada out of business. The pathetic story of the furniture industry is pretty well set out in the price spreads report, from which I wild quote, because in my opinion the question of tariff has nothing to do with the matter at all. I will read just two or three extracts from the report of the prioe spreads commission with regard to the furniture manufacturing industry:
Coincident, however, with the growth of furniture factories was a concentration in retail distribution which led to the elimination of more and more independent outlets. In the city of Winnipeg during the past twelve or fifteen years approximately one furniture dealer per annum has ceased business and at the present time there remains only one dealer aside from the department stores.
The same story may be told of nearly every city in Canada. Then the report goes on:
... it became of paramount importance to every manufacturer to sell to the department stores. The concentration of purchasing power in the hand's of the latter undoubtedly intensified competition and accentuated the severity of the necessary adjustment.
I will ask the house to note what is said in conclusion, in view of the suggestion that the furniture industry is to be injured by a lowering of the tariff from forty-five per cent to twenty-seven per cent:
... this industry presents an illustration of a completely disorganized body of producers.... The field of retail distribution of the industry's product is, however, dominated by a few department stores, giving rise to a wide disparity in bargaining power between the producer and the distributor of furniture.
