The result of such disparity, combined with over-extension of production facilities, has been to drive prices to a point well below the proper cost of production with a consequent impairment not only of the manufacturer's capital, but of the standard of living of the wage-earner.
I refer to that particularly because it indicates that the question of the tariff has nothing to do with the welfare of that industry. It is a domestic question and a matter of their own practice in control of their own business.

Just in conclusion, sir, may I say that in my opinion the proper course to follow is to give this agreement a chance. Let us see whether it will work. The government has promised great things from this treaty, and the country is looking for great results. I would say to the government that the measure of success attained will depend largely upon the manner in which this agreement is administered.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is my first opportunity to do so I should like to extend my congratulations to you and to the deputy speaker of the house upon your appointment to the high positions .which you occupy.
As I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and to the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), I could not help but, think how great minds change. I well recall that when the Minister of Finance first came to parliament he entered this house as more or less of a free trader from western Canada. This afternoon, however, he reserved the right, when the intermediate tariff is dealt with in the budget, to revise it either upward or downward. 'Twixt the wheat fields of Saskatchewan and the lights of St. James street his policy has altered almost as rapidly as his location has changed. As I listened to the hon. member for Kootenay East, who also supported this proposed agreement, I could not help but recall the vigorous protectionist speeches made by the hon. gentleman in other days.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Now the hon.
gentleman is presenting an equally vigorous defence on behalf of the low tariff party. I am reminded of those words which have been set to music, "What a difference just a few years make." I am not surprised that one who has changed so often should perhaps prefer not to refer to the records of the two major political parties in this country.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am glad to anticipate certain advantages which may accrue from the proposed agreement, but I am alarmed when I consider the serious dangers that threaten the economic life and national outlook of Canada. I have heard it said in the house that this achievement is the dream of Laurier Liberalism come true; I have heard it said that this agreement has been brought about through the good feeling that has been established between the two countries. No matter how much one might be tempted to do so, however, I do not think any hon. member on either side of the house should claim that his party is the only one

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
that desires a reasonable increase in trade with the United States. I have read many of the debates that have taken place in this chamber; I have listened to speakers on both sides for ten or eleven sessions and I am satisfied that ever since confederation every party in the house has had an underlying desire for a closer trade relationship with the United States. More than that, practically every party has made definite efforts to that end. Some have merely clamored for more trade on a free trade basis; others have advocated fair trade; others have supported reciprocity at any price, while still others have insisted that any agreement or reciprocity must be one that would reciprocate advantages to Canadians as well as to Americans.
I know that for a long time there has been a difference of thought as between high and low tariffs but, as someone has well said, any agreement is popular at its inception. Therefore I hesitate to forecast the ill effects that I believe may result from this agreement, because for a long time the idea of some such agreement has been very popular in the public mind. However, if there is any one thing more conspicuous than the spectacular manner in which this agreement was speedily ushered into this house, it is the evident lack of consideration that was given to it. Why, on the part of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) it was only a holiday affair; it took him only forty-eight hours to negotiate an agreement which for forty-eight years his party had failed to bring into effect.
I do not intend to go into all the details of this agreement. They have been well covered by my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett) and well explained from the other point of view by the right hon. Prime Minister, but I feel in duty bound to point out to the house some of the general principles involved as well as the reason why I propose to vote against this agreement. I intend to express my lack of confidence in the fiscal policies of the Liberal party and to deal with a few of the details of the agreement which I believe threaten the economic independence and national outlook of this country.
It is true, as has been well said, that we live in close proximity to a country speaking our language, having the same customs, and with similar standards of living. Interchange of goods, views and even influence during the years has been much more convenient than would have been the case had our traditions been more foreign and our geographical location more distant. We find our trade has developed enormously; even without any agreements we have had an enormous volume of trade with the United States for many years. Canada
has achieved the unique position of being the greatest foreign customer of that vast republic. The Prime Minister of Canada has for many years been a champion of friendly relations with the United States and has repeatedly expressed the underlying desire of Canadians for the closest possible relations with that country. Little need be said about our peaceful relations with the United States; for over one hundred years we have maintained a relationship based upon a desire for international peace, a relationship closer than exists probably between any other two countries.
But it has been said, and said truly, that there is no sentiment in business; that statement I believe has never been challenged. I think it is equally true that bad trade arrangements and unsound trade policies have never improved relations between any two nations. There are in trade elements that are important and vital, and one of the most important is regularity and stability. We have no particular assurance of any stability, regularity or continuity of demand in trade with the United States. As I look back over our history-and I am not afraid to look back; I look back sometimes to get more light that I may see further ahead-and when I think of the trade agreement we had with the United States from 1854 to 1866, the oldest trade agreement and the only one that ever stood with that country, which was cut off abruptly, I read of how our pioneer forefathers were forced to struggle for their livelihood when they found that trade which had been established north and south suddenly cut off. Everyone knows that the cutting off of that trade was a considerable factor in bringing about confederation, and led to the establishment of a transcontinental railway and to a national fiscal policy, a national plan for our development east and west, because our fathers saw the danger of building on the shifting sand of a market controlled by another country. With that in view we find that immediately after 1866 when that trade was cut off these other developments that, after all, are the fundamental features of our national structure were established. From that day on, from Quebec to British Columbia, we have steadily developed our trade east and west; the transcontinental railways, which those who still desired trade north and south forecast would not pay for the axle grease, were made to pay and served the great provinces of the west, and that development east and west has been such as to make it possible for the Prime Minister, as head of the sixth trading nation of the world, now to negotiate with a great foreign power.
Among the factors involved in this issue are trade, transportation and employment. I
Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement

shudder to think of the effect upon our great transportation systems that are to-day operating with difficulty, when under this agreement trade is encouraged to flow north and south rather than east and west, when the short haul of the United States roads to serve western Canada from the cites of the central states replaces the haul from our eastern cities, which I believe it must be said in all fairness have done fairly well by assistance to the western provinces. It might reasonably be expected that north and south trade would develop markets for us when we remember that there are some 125 million people to the south of us while we have only about 11 million here, but I am amazed to find that in the last forty years we have purchased from the United States every year $150,000,000 more in value of goods than we have sold to them. Let us pause to imagine what that means, a total of $6,000,000,000, double the national debt, equal to the total agricultural production of Canada every six years. That is what we have paid for our trade with the United States, and we still owe them $1,000,000 in carrying charges on our debt every day the sun sets. This great trade has been established, why? Because the United States, just as in this trade agreement, have seen to it all down through the years that they supply us with the finished products of the labouring men of the United States and receive from us more in volume of raw products but less in value until processed by American labour. Not even the minister who smiles can deny that the advantages secured in this agreement, which are very small, are for our raw products and only to a very limited degree even at that.

speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I was smiling at his speech, and wondering if he had been in favour of the agreement his leader tried to negotiate.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I can only say that I have followed my leader longer than the hon. minister has ever followed any leader. I believe in trade east and west, trade that will develop Canada for the Canadian people. I have no apology to make for any of our slogans in the past, no apology for any of our policies in the past, no apology for the encouragement of trade that assists our own ports instead of American ports, no apology for policies that assist our own labour rather than American labour. I have reason for lacking confidence in the present government's fiscal policy, because even you, Mr. Speaker, before you dropped your political affiliations, realized full well, looking back over the path-
way of Liberal fiscal policy that it was a path strewn with fear, failure and uncertainty. When I think of its winding, changing course in the fiscal affairs of this dominion, I say "fear" advisedly. The Prime Minister smiles. I do not mean to say that he is fearful under all circumstances. I have seen him quite brave in parliament; I have seen him quite brave in the country, and I congratulate him upon his success. But I find as I look back over the record that Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie, and his former leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, warned us against trade policies that would annoy or irritate the United States. Then prior to 1930, when American tariff increases were being discussed and the present Prime Minister was urged by those on this side of the house to raise our tariffs against the United States I remember him saying: No, we must not do anything for fear it might be considered provocative in the United States at this time.
When the Prime Minister spoke a few days ago he went into details, covering two pages of Hansard, in outlining his policy of fear, in which he stated that if we did not negotiate the agreement immediately, the United States threatened to retaliate; that they would raise their tariffs, placing them in the general column, an innovation in tariff practice which the right hon. gentleman explained. He said, further, that apart from the treaty he was fearful that the United States might retaliate by higher tariffs unless we reduced our tariffs in some way or made it possible by our intermediate tariff arrangements and regulations to allow trade to come in through American as well as Canadian ports. In the view of the right hon. gentleman to do otherwise might be costly to our newsprint industry, in that newsprint might no longer be exported to the United States unless we accepted this agreement.
To-day as I listened to the Minister of Finance it appeared to me that evidently he has been contaminated by that feature of the policy, and that he was also fearful of retaliation from the United States. When we consider the history of Canada all through the years we find that more or less that has been the policy of the Liberal party endeavouring to consummate United States agreements; that all through the years they have emphasized to a greater or lesser degree that we should not irritate or annoy that country. We received the warning about not being provocative to the United States at a time when we were buying a million dollars worth of goods more from them each day than we were selling to them. Canada changed

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
her favourable trade balance of over S400,-
000.000 in 1926 to an unfavourable trade balance of over $100,000,000 in 1930. During that period we did not increase our unfavourable trade balance by $150,000,000, as was mentioned previously, as an average, but were buying over $300,000,000-in fact, in 1929 I believe it was over $400,000,000-more from the United States than we sold them. The Prime Minister knows as well as does any other hon. member that during those years almost half a million of our boys and girls went to the United States to find employment.
These are serious national matters, of great concern to the dominion. I know it would not be expected by hon. members to your right, and overflowing to your left, Mr. Speaker, that I would have much confidence in the fiscal policy of the Liberal party. But I say in all kindness to each individual of that large, unwieldy and possibly temporary force that the policy of their party so far as trade relations are concerned has changed many times. I have read where leaders as great as Hon. George Brown left the Conservative party, after the government of that day tried so hard to renew the treaty that had been cut off in 1866. He left it and joined the Liberal party because the late Sir John A. Macdonald offered too much on behalf of the Canadian government. Later, that same Liberal party, which at one time thought not enough was being offered and another time thought we offered too much, changed to unrestricted reciprocity. Then later, by name alone it followed a policy of commercial union with the United States. On down through the years we find those different suggestions dying; one by one; some died in parliament; some died in congress; some died before they got to congress and others died in the country. In 1911 reciprocity died before the vote of the people, and I venture to say that if this trade agreement were presented to the Canadian people in the light in which it has been presented to this chamber it would not carry a majority of the votes of this country to-day.
One could name many more instances, but I would hesitate to do so. We know however that such a great leader of the Liberal party as Sir Richard Cartwright took a definite stand in the matter. One can trace a changing Liberal doctrine all down through the years. The late Sir Richard Cartwright said that we must have unrestricted reciprocity with the United States, no matter what the cost may be. He said, "We will have it, no matter what the cost is." Twitted in parliament and asked
if he did not think this would affect our trade with the United Kingdom he said, "Yes, and the only way to get it is by raising your tariff all along the line against every country on the face of the world, even the United Kingdom as well."
Well, to-day we find the doctrine of the Liberal party has been emphasized, and was emphasized particularly during the election. To-day that party is one which stands for the lowering of tariffs all along the line, a policy which is proposed by the right hon. the prime minister to be the only proper basis for trade negotiation. I pause to urge hon. members to watch carefully the budget which will be brought down by the Minister of Finance, in view of the fact that to-day he told the house that he reserved the right to raise or lower duties. As a one time free trader he now stands as a protection valve, to repair tariffs lowered by his leader. He now stands ready to apply emergency measures he may consider necessary to restore an equalizing effect upon Canada in view of the situation brought about by the freer trade inclinations of the Prime Minister. I know many other changes, and especially the ones respecting the imperial trade relationships, could be mentioned.
While the late Sir Richard Cartwright would even tax Great Britain in order to have trade with the United States, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said, "There shall be no more pilgrimages to Washington," and he turned his attention to the motherland. What did he do? He gave a preference to the motherland, and did not ask anything from them. Yet to-day the Prime Minister-

speechtext: Certainly he was opposed by the Tories; the new member is right. He was opposed by the Tories and by Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper. Sir Charles Tupper stated that he believed in reciprocal trade arrangements with the old land, as well, which would give equal advantages to Canada and England.

speechtext: Knowing he could not get it.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
My hon. friend should look back and remember what happened. The present leader of the government knows that between 1899 and 1905 one-third of the textile industry of Canada went out of business and thousands lost their jobs because the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was too generous to England, and had he followed Sir

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
Charles Tupper's advice the textile industry of Canada would not have received the death blow she did receive at that time.
The present prime minister did not suggest that we should give the motherland preferences and receive nothing, but he refused to support the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) who brought the imperial trade agreements before this chamber. He refused to support a preference for England when Canada was securing more by way of preference than the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier ever expected to receive or any Canadian had even hoped for. When I speak about the imperial trade agreements I notice the Prime Minister laughs, but my reply is that he who laughs last laughs best. If he and I are spared for two or three years-and I hope we shall be-we may have an opportunity to compare the advantages derived from the imperial trade agreements with the disadvantages Canada will suffer from the Canada-United States agreement now before us. Keep my words in mind, because I say to every hon. member within sound of my voice that if he has given any thought to the imperial trade agreements he must agree with me that had it not been for them agriculture, the great basic industry of Canada, would be bankrupt to-day. I urge hon. members to consider that point carefully.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) placed on Hansard details which I shall not repeat. I shall be content with saying that the advantages we secured in the motherland had the effect of stabilizing our markets. I shall mention only one example of stabilization, although in fact many could be cited. There is not an hon. member experienced in agriculture who would not agree with the statement that since the imperial trade agreements became effective we have had a more stabilized price for bacon than at any other time since confederation. Any farmer knows what that means. Even the Minister of Finance himself, who 'has been removed from the pursuit of agriculture for some time, will agree that there is nothing more important for the Canadian mixed farmer than a stabilized price for his products. But the imperial trade agreements did not do only that. They provided us with advantages in the greatest market in the world, and the one in which we can hope for the greatest stability.
What have we received in this agreement? As I listened to the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) I wondered why he should have a change of heart now and accept this agreement as something that was going to bring great benefits to Canada. Lumber has been mentioned. It is true that

under this agreement we can send our lumber to the United States at a lower rate of duty, not free but at a reduced rate, and then only in limited quotas, but in return we tell the manufacturers of the United States that they can ship their furniture into Canada, not in limited quantities, but as much as they like, free of duty.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the criminal code (fines and penalties).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of this particular bill, copies of which are on mem-bler's files, is to provide that fines imposed under the criminal code may be paid on time or by instalment, the conditions to be laid down by the magistrates or judges after inquiring into the ability of the accused to pay. Owing to five years of depression many people on relief and out of work, or on part time, many of them first offenders with families and some of them returned soldiers, cannot pay their fines, and have to go to gaol,- which is another way of imposing imprisonment for debt. The bill follows the provision of the law of England, 1935, 25-26 George V, chapter 46, known as Money Payments (Justices Procedure Act), 1935.
The first section of the bill is partly new matter; the other sections are entirely new. The first section in the bill amends section 1029 of the criminal code, "fine or penalty in discretion of court":
Wherever a fine may be awarded or a penalty imposed for any offence, the amount of such fine or penalty shall, within such limits, if any, as are prescribed in that behalf, be in the discretion of the court or person passing sentence or convicting, as the case may be.
Sections 1036, 1037 and 1038 of the code deal with fines and forfeitures.
The first section of the bill is entirely new, and all the other sections follow the law of England. This matter came up in Great Britain two years ago. It was dealt with by a committee of parliament and a departmental inquiry, and this particular act which is now the law of England came into force on January 1 and is working well in the old country.
During times of depression people get out of work and, if convicted, cannot pay their fines, with the result that they have to go to gaol. Many of them have families.

Criminal Code-Fines and Penalties
The British Money Payments Act was introduced in the House of Lords on July 11. It went over to the House of Commons on August 2, and received the royal assent. It was supported by all parties in both houses of parliament, and the judges who took part in the debate in the House of Lords spoke strongly in favour of this measure. This whole question, Mr. Speaker, is wrapped up in the liberty of the subject, and after all is said and done, Britain is the only country in which there is real liberty to-day.
As I view the situation, the term "liberty" is becoming meaningless in Canada, with imprisonment of thousands for debt, with trial by newspaper supplanting trial by jury, with the difficulty of getting bail, with the almost kingly powers which parliament and the provinces have conferred upon magistrates. It is all right to read of a conception embodied in text-books on the law of evidence two or three hundred years old, but it needs to be brought up to date and rewritten, when you have a magistrate committing a man for trial, a grand jury finding a prima facie case is made out on the facts, and along coming a judge who, not satisfied with telling the jury what the law is-which is his proper function-takes the case from the jury, often supplanting trial by jury. We have cases about the fourth estate affecting reports of this parliament, reports of committees; freedom of the press is assailed openly in Canada to-day.
This bill deals with an important question of law reform. It is one of the greatest problems affecting this country at the present time. Law reforms here are away behind the times; we have to go to the motherland, the land of the free, and see what they are doing over there. We find they are getting back to the principles of magna charta, the principles of the Petition of Right, following right away down to the statute of Westminster. Throughout we find the principle of the liberty of the subject. In Canada the liberty of the subject does not extend very far. Certain people outside this house can snap their fingers at parliament; they can even say to a newspaper "We will cut off your advertising if you dare to publish the truth, or publish what goes on in the debates of this house or its committees."
I do not ask that the government shall immediately adopt this bill. I believe we should follow the procedure of the mother of parliaments, in which, prior to the act to which I referred last August being placed on the statute books, it was admitted that the case was proven and they appointed a
departmental committee. Besides having as its chairman a distinguished lawyer, Sir John Fischer Williams, K.C., the committee also comprised a former chairman of the prison commission, a former metropolitan magistrate, . a leading stipendiary magistrate and a justice's clerk. They went into this whole question and presented a report to both houses of parliament, with the result that this act was placed on the statute books of the motherland. I think we should do well to have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) appoint a parliamentary committee or a departmental committee to deal with this whole problem of law reform.
After all is said and done, what is Liberalism? As we have it to-day it does not exist along these lines, when we see that "liberty" is just a meaningless term in this country. As I said, this bill is wrapped up with the liberty of the subject. Imprisonment for debt was abolished in England and Wales by act of parliament in 1869; yet in 1923, according to a report of the House of Lords, 23,000 people were imprisoned for failure to pay sums of money. In 1910 the number was 90,000, although imprisonment for debt had been abolished for forty years. Figures show that only twenty-seven per cent of the men and twenty-one per cent of the women imprisoned in England had been convicted of indictable crimes; the rest had made default in payments of money and had been convicted of breaches of various acts, regulations and bylaws with respect to which imprisonment with or without the option of a fine could be imposed.
When a man is sent to gaol in default of payment of a fine he is not the only person who suffers. His family suffers; his children suffer through the bread-winner being in gaol; his reputation suffers; he may lose his job, and then it is hard for him to get another. In England last year 11,000 people had to go to gaol because they were unable to pay fines. An attempt has been made to remove this state of affairs through the new statute to which I have referred.
The bill which I propose will need the support also of the provinces. It deals with offences under the criminal code just as far as the legislative competence of this parliament goes. In addition, the provinces should pass complementary legislation. The practice at present is as follows: A fine is first imposed. Under my bill there will be an amendment whereunder the fine will be fixed first, and if default occurs in payment an inquiry will be made by the judge or the magistrate as to the ability and capacity of the defendant to

Criminal Code-Fines and Penalties
pay, and his means in relation to the amount involved. A prison term will be ordered only if the court thinks it wise. That is modern, humane legislation.
As a result of a similar law, Mr. Speaker, half the prisons are closed in the old country, at a great saving to the state, for seventy-five per cent of persons in English prisons were imprisoned for debt and only about twenty-five per cent for indictable offences. Imprisonment is a most expensive luxury for the state. Also it is harsh and severe in its consequences to the individual; it has a bad effect upon a man's character and his self-respect. It causes suffering to his family and dependents, interruption of his work, and the possibility of failure to find work upon his release- penalties often out of all proportion to the wrong which the offender has committed or the fault of which he has been found guilty. Such a penalty should never be imposed without careful consideration and only resorted to if it is the only practical way of vindicating the law of the land or enforcing obligations which must be enforced. It should never be imposed in the mechanical or autocratic way that prevails at present.
The peak of imprisonment for debt in this country seems to coincide with times of great industrial depression. The figures indicate this clearly. It is most regrettable that unemployment should result in the imprisonment of men because they are unable to fulfil obligations contracted for when they were at work; that they should be forced to comply with a court order which is based upon their earnings when they were employed. I think it is also regrettable that there are so few methods of dealing with offenders; that such methods are limited to the ones used three hundred years ago, namely, fines and imprisonment.
In his work The New Despotism, Lord Ilewart has referred to this matter. It seems to me that at last the British government has written finis to Little Dorrit, Dickens' novel criticizing the conditions he described a century ago, from personal knowledge of the debtors' prison in London. Little Dorrit herself ministered there, and of the conditions Sam Weller said, "It's unekal, and that's the fault on it." In 1869, stirred by Dickens' description of these conditions, the government of England brought down an act prohibiting imprisonment for debt. Nevertheless to-day nearly half the commitments to prison, though nominally on account of what is known as contempt of court, are actually for non-payment of money liabilities.
The action now being taken is intended to change this state of affairs. First the gov-

eminent appointed a departmental committee; then the matter went to the House of Lords and the House of Commons, and the bill passed both houses unanimously, and was supported by the press all over England. They circularized the magistrates and judges and obtained full information before the act was passed. I should like to read one or two press clippings in regard to this matter:
The Earl of Faversham announced this on behalf of the government in the house of Lords. The government's object, Lord Faversham said, was that there should be "no delay whatsoever in bringing to the notice of all courts of summary jurisdiction suggestions and considerations which may tend to reduce the number of imprisonments and may assist courts to confine the use of this extreme measure to eases where it is unavoidable if the authority of the courts is to be properly upheld."
This statement was the climax to a debate initiated by Lord Arnold, Labour party peer, who called attention to the report made last autumn by a government committee on this question. Lord Arnold said that in 1932 no less than 24,272 persons in the United Kingdom were sent to prison for non-payment of fines, maintenance orders, local taxes and other monetary demands.
In one case, he said, a youth was sent to prison as the indirect outcomei of swinging in a public park in the wrong swing. The young man had been fined. He was careless, and because the fine was not paid, and _ perhaps could not be paid, he had to go to prison. In another, a man was similarly imprisoned for failure to pay a fine imposed upon him for sleeping in an automobile upon a public road.
Baron Merrivale, a lord justice of appeal, confirmed the fact that such a state of things existed. It had come to an end practically for well-to-do people a century ago. Lord Merrivale said, but it had not come to an end for "the poor people who are the subject of these various orders."
Baron Snell, late member of the Imperial Economic Committee, pointed out that Britain has much to learn on this question from the United States. "When I was in America a year or two ago," he said, a judge of the supreme court was good enough to express to me in the most emphatic way his admiration and the admiration of American jurists generally for the common law of England."
In this parliament we should always be on our guard in order to do nothing that will take away from the liberty of the subject. When we look at Europe, where there is no longer any liberty in the legislatures, the press, the pulpits or the universities, more than ever we should stand on guard to see that the principles of magna charta are not violated. They are being violated in this country to-day; in fact I should like to know where the magna charta exists at the present time. The development of this liberty took many centuries; it was achieved at great cost both individually and to the state. One principle of the great charter was that no free man should be arrested or detained in

Criminal Code-Fines and Penalties
prison, or outlawed or banished or brought to ruin, save by the judgment of his peers and in accordance with the law of the land. On the other hand we have taxation without representation, and liberty is being restricted all along the line, with the vast powers now enjoyed by the magistrates, with the jury system supplanted by newspaper trials and all that sort of thing. Where is the Magna Charta when people are sent down for nonpayment of small fines?
Our whole system of freedom, as we have it to-day throughout the British empire and the United States, is based upon the subjection of the executive and its ministers to the law of the land, and one of our cardinal principles is that the courts are subservient to the legislature. Look at the United States; where is liberty there? What has happened to the liberty of the subject over there? In this country, too, those ties which bind us to the motherland seem to be weakening. In the United States they suffer from politics and lawlessness, kidnappers, racketeering and all that sort of thing, and to a certain extent we suffer from the same conditions. The square deal of Theodore Roosevelt and the new freedom of Woodrow Wilson 'have been absolutely swept away. So much is this the case that a distinguished citizen of the United States, Colonel Lindbergh, had to leave the land of the free and the home of the brave for a really free country, the only one in the world to-day.
I would suggest to the minister that he follow the practice that has been followed in the old country, and institute a departmental inquiry into these questions. He is a very efficient minister, and he has always been receptive to suggestions coming from the opposition, though it is true that he sent the new deal, the new freedom, to the law courts. In this country, as I say, the courts are subservient, or should be, to the legislatures, and I believe the time is not far distant when we shall have to reassert the principle enunciated by Theodore Roosevelt at Chicago in 1912, when he said, "The American people, not the courts, should determine their own policies." The court of last resort is 'the people, and this high court of parliament could accomplish no greater work than to protect the liberty of the people. This should be even more so now that we have twentieth century Liberalism in Canada. I am afraid, however, that twentieth century Liberalism and economic Liberalism in .this country are nothing but myths.
I hope the minister will give serious consideration to this bill, which is patterned after
the English act now in force. I should be glad to send the minister a copy of the English bill, which is contained in a book entitled Imprisonment by Justices for Non-Payment of Money, written by Wallace Thoday, who is a member of the bar, and published at Mansion House, London, December, 1935. I suggest that in this connection the minister should consult the municipalities also, because after all is said and done the municipalities, rather than the provinces, should receive all the fines. All fines levied under the criminal code should belong exclusively to the municipalities. Parliament gives the provinces subsidies for the maintenance of provincial institutions, while the municipalities have to maintain the .police forces, which in some cities cost .two or two and a half million dollars. Australia gives a subvention to her capital city for the maintenance of the police force there. A few years ago parliament conferred upon the provinces the right to collect these fines, subject to an agreement to be made with the municipalities. Some fines go to the provinces, many to the municipalities, but all these fines should go to the municipality, to the authority which not only enforces the law but prosecutes.
In my opinion the time has come for reform. I should like to hear from the minister whether he is agreeable to acting along the line taken by the mother of parliaments, where they found a condition under twentieth century Liberalism that 24,000 people were in prison for non-payment of debt. In any event during the depression there should be a suspension of imprisonment for non-payment of fines, and time given to pay. Before a fine is imposed this bill provides that a magistrate should make inquiry as to the ability of the accused to pay. It is not only the man himself who suffers; if he loses his job the wife and family suffer. In Toronto forty-five years ago the late R. J. Fleming when chairman of the board of police commissioners passed a by-law allowing the police inspector discretion to release a man arrested for drunkenness, with the result that he could go to his work in the morning. By that humane provision he saved many a family from suffering. I hope the minister will be in a receptive mood and follow the example of the motherland. If he admires Liberalism as they have it in the old land let him follow them in that respect. The government of the day is responsible to the electors of the country for bringing about such necessary reforms. These reforms are in the public interest and protect the liberty of the subject, which is becoming an almost meaningless term in this country.

Criminal Code-Fines and Penalties
Hon, ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice): The main section of this bill, which is section 1, would give discretion to a court or to a person imposing a fine or penalty to allow time for the payment of that fine, and even to order that the amount may be paid by instalments, at times, in amounts and under such conditions as the case may require. This is the most important section of the bill. Fundamentally I do not see any objection to the principle of this section. I understand that certain magistrates even now purport to do this although there is no statutory authority that allows it. But the difficulty would be to devise a law which, while giving this discretion in cases where it may be properly exercised, would have the necessary safeguards to prevent those who could pay from escaping part of their sentence.
Ini 19291 there was introduced in the other house by Senator Beaubien a bill of this kind containing exactly the same provision as appears in this section. I have before me the debates of that year in the other house, and there were objections raised to that provision. The bill was withdrawn. I call attention to the fact that in the explanatory note to the bill now before the house my hon. friend says that this legislation is advisable owing to the five years of depression which have caused many people to be on relief or out of work. The bill in the other house was introduced in 1929, at the peak of the boom. At any rate the principle of my hon. friend's bill is not entirely new. But as I say, there is nothing which seems specially objectionable in this provision so long as the section is drafted in such a way as to provide all necessary safeguards.
Section 2 of the bill provides for new sections 1029A and 1029B. I must confess I cannot see that those sections would be very valuable, and there are objections to them from certain viewpoints.
As to section 1029C, if the first section were accepted this should be accepted also. It provides that when a convicted person would have paid part of the penalty, if he could not pay the balance and had to serve a term in gaol, the term of imprisonment should be reduced because of the amount of fine he has paid.
As to section 3 of the bill, which would enact two new sections, 1057A and 1057B, I would not only be inclined but have to oppose this section. By section 1057A a court which has power to pass a sentence of imprisonment^
-in lieu of passing a sentence of imprisonment, may order that the offender he detained within the precincts of the court, or at any police station, till such hour, not later than eight in the evening on the day on which he is convicted, as the court may direct.

And the court-
-shall not make any such order of detention under this section as will deprive the offender of a reasonable opportunity of returning to his abode on the day on which such order of detention is made.
Well, I am a friend of liberty, as my hon. friend is, but this would be almost killing the offender with kindness. If I correctly understand this section the court would not even sentence the prisoner-or he is not a prisoner, because this is for the purpose of preventing him from going to gaol-but instead of passing sentence the court would merely order that he be detained within the precincts until not later than eight o'clock in the evening.
The hon. member said that the bill before us is based upon the English Money Payments Act of 1935. I suggest however that it goes much further than the English act. Under that act the court which has adjudged the sum to be paid by the accused, in lieu of issuing a warrant immediately may order that he be detained in the police station until he can obtain the money to pay the amount of his fine. In the proposal of the hon. member, however, there is no such provision. Instead1 of passing sentence on a man the court would simply order that he be detained "within the precincts of the court, or at any police station, till such hour, not later than eight in the evening on the day on which he is convicted." I do not think it would be worth while for any person to make a complaint and secure such a conviction.
Then, section 1067B is along the same lines. It would enact that:
(2) Where a person is liable to be sentenced to imprisonment by a court of summary jurisdiction, the court may, if any suitable places are available for the purpose, order the person to be detained within the precincts of the court or at any police station for such period not exceeding four days as the court thinks fit, and the order shall be delivered with the offender to the person in charge of the place where the offender is to be detained.
That section would prescribe that no person shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a period of less than five days. When the sentence is less than five days, the judge would order that the person be detained within the precincts of the court or at a police station, instead of going to gaol. I must object to the two proposal® contained in section 3 of the bill.
I suggest to the hon. member, however, that in Canada the administration of criminal justice is under the control of the provinces. The officers who have the experience in these matters are the attorneys general of the various provinces. They are the officers who are responsible, and I should like to submit

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
to the law officers of the different provinces the proposal contained in the hon. member's bill. Upon consultation with them it might be possible, as I stated before, that section 1 and part of section 2 might be accepted. Either such provisions might be included in the bill which will be introduced by the government to amend the criminal code or, if the hon. member would prefer, his bill might be allowed to stand until I receive the advice of the various legal authorities of the provinces as to the merits of the provisions in the bill. Under those circumstances we would be able to proceed and give to the hon. member the amount of satisfaction his proposal deserves.

Mr. Speaker, I gladly accept the suggestion offered by the minister. As I said before, I did not expect the bill would be passed until such time as it had been considered by the provincial attorneys general and by officials of municipalities as to how it may affect the payment of fines. I would be the last person to propose interfering in that regard, 'because I have always contended that fines belong to the municipalities. I would suggest that the bill stand over, and that the minister incorporate it in the general amendments to the criminal code which will be brought down later in the session. Meantime the minister could consult representatives of the provinces.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) will place
me, after I have finished speaking, whether he will put me on the gangway which he has created, or in some other place. I am sure, however, that he will know exactly where I stand, and what I think about the trade agreement now under discussion.
While I have no further observations concerning the hon. member for Danforth I have one or two respecting the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). In the first instance he took exception to the speech made by the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens). He recalled some protectionist speeches which in years gone by had been made by that hon. member. I could not help thinking that had the fortunes of war favoured the Conservative party and had they been sitting on the right side of Mr. Speaker the hon. member would have been one of the first to have echoed the speech made by the hon. member for East Kootenay, and would not have been deploring the fact that we have a treaty giving us trade relations with the United States.
He spoke, further, regarding the haste displayed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in consummating and completing the agreement. If the Prime Minister had delayed much longer and if the agreement had not been completed and we were not discussing it at this time I can assure hon. members that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe would have raised his hand in holy horror because of the delay of the Prime Minister in completing an agreement so far advanced by his own party.
If in my observations I have to deal with statements already made I do so because this seems necessary from the western standpoint, and I do not use the term in a parochial sense but rather from the point of view of the dominion. The debate of this measure seems to me somewhat like preparatory service to the communion on the budget. Most of those who have spoken have been dealing with the matter from that standpoint, as a preliminary to the budget, because you will find, Mr. Speaker, that most of the remarks are addressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and he is somewhat . on the defensive and is endeavouring as best he can to conceal his thoughts as to what might be contained in the budget.
There is one feature of this debate, however, that I am rather glad to see, and that is that we have an opportunity of discussing the principles of protection and free trade so early in the session rather than on the eve of an election, and in this debate, before we are through we shall find just what are the bases of the principles upon which each of the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
parties made their appeal to the country. I do not know whether ever in the history of Canada before there has been a situation such as we have here where the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has made to a neighbouring government proposals along the lines of a treaty. The only parallel that I know of is one which took place, I think in 1867, when Mr. Gladstone through his government was introducing an extension of the Franchise Act, which Mr. Disraeli was then opposing. In the subsequent election, and chiefly on the ground of his opposition to the Franchise Act, Mr. Disraeli was returned to power, and then when he came into office, with a cynical indifference to consistency he passed that very bill of Mr. Gladstone's and, in fact, extended its provisions. In the present case the situation is somewhat different. The present leader of the opposition had as Prime Minister made certain proposals to the United States government and these proposals had Seen under consideration for some considerable time by the permanent officers of the two governments and by the then Prime Minister himself. For some reason or another the response that was made by the United States was not such as the then Prime Minister wished. Then when the late government was turned out on October 14, a new Prime Minister took office, and with the sanction and the entire concurrence of the people of Canada he immediately approached the United States government with a view to a trade treaty. In that treaty he was able to embody a great many of the proposals set forth by the present leader of the opposition, and the present Prime Minister was able to complete the treaty within a remarkably short time.
May I say that in my judgment it might have been well if the leader of the opposition had taken the position that Mr. Gladstone took when Mr. Disraeli's government brought in the franchise bill. Mr. Gladstone supported it, and I do think the leader of the opposition might have been well advised to approve this treaty as he certainly had a great deal to do with its framework. However, he did not do so, and so we are met with his opposition to the bill, which opposition has been replied to in extenso, I think, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to-day. The Minister of Finance to-day gave to the house these uncontroverted and incontestable facts, that the provisions of the treaty were initiated in the proposals of the leader of the opposition, and that, despite what was said by the leader of the opposition in his speech the other day, these proposals have been completed by this government.

I remember hearing the leader of the opposition make a radio address last September. It was the only address I heard him make during the course of the campaign, and it was given, I think, on a Friday or Saturday night. This is what he said-I have a copy of his remarks here:
You say: "But you have not mentioned the trading situation with the United States." I have not, but I now will. It has been said by my opponents, and particularly by my opponents in the west, that the Bennett government did not desire to trade with the United States, that the Bennett government had no realization of the need of securing for our primary producers greater markets in that great country, and that therefore we were making no effort to obtain them.
It was said that we had a brief for the industrialists and didn't care a hang about our agriculturalists. And that consequently we were just going through the motions of trading with our good friends to the south.
Well, that does not happen to be the ease. Ever since this government has been in office, it has done everything possible to increase our trade with the United States. We have consistently expressed our willingness to give concessions for concessions granted. Before June, 1934, by the then only practicable means available, we did all that was possible to secure greater entry for our natural products in that great market. When, in June. 1934, Congress gave to the president of the United States powers to conclude trade agreements, this government was eager to take advantage of what it regarded as this new and better opportunity to increase its exports. It acted accordingly. Note this fact carefully. What specifically this government did. and the nature of its proposals, will be made knowrn to you through the publication of a certain document. This publication will be made on Monday next.
This document will be my answer to the unfair-minded people who, knowing better, still maintain that this government has never seriously attempted to do business with the United ' States. Set up the statements of my political foes against the written statement which you will read; and learn in time how little dependability can be put upon the words of the leaders of Liberalism.
So much for that, to-night. But carefully examine this document.
Well, it happened that I was addressing a meeting that night, and I ventured into the realm of prophecy, as a rule a very unsafe place to tread. I then stated on that platform, as I stated on every platform during that campaign, that there would be no trade treaty with the United States through the instrumentality of the then Prime Minister. I said that he would make the approaches, but he could not and he would not give the concessions that would be demanded by the president of the United States.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
I further stated on every
platform that there was only one party and only one man in the dominion who could

Camda-TJ. S. Trade Agreement
complete a trade agreement with the president of the United States, and that party was the Liberal party, and that man was the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I stated my reasons also. I said that I knew something of the mentality of the right hon. leader of the opposition. I knew the environment in which he had lived during most of the years of his manhood; I knew from his speeches in the house and on the hustings that there was no possibility of any agreement being consummated by him just because of his mentality. He had indicated that in the house and in committee.
Some hon. members who were in this chamber at the time will remember that when the grain board was being constituted and the leader of the opposition's own friend, Mr. James Richardson, was giving evidence, Mr. Richardson stated that he could sell fifty million bushels of grain at seventy cents a bushel, whereupon the chairman of the committee, the right hon. leader of the opposition, said, "What then?" The reply was that we must purchase the goods of those countries in which we sell our wheat. The leader of the opposition replied: "The same old story," that the goods of the industries of the United States would flood the markets of Canada. At that particular moment, when they were dealing with the affairs of the farmers of Canada, the then Prime Minister made it absolutely clear to the country that what he was concerned with was the rights, as he thought, and the privileges of the industrialists. I think the statement that he made in his radio address that they were concerned only with the industrialists was entirely true because he has consistently taken the position that he has saved Canada during the last five years; in the saving of Canada he has pointed to the protection that he has given to the industrialists of the east, and in that way he believes he has saved Canada.
I am going to suggest that the leader of the opposition is not a very good logician. I remember when I was studying logic it was always clearly brought to my attention that you could never draw a universal conclusion with a minor premise in the syllogism. He has taken the position and he has drawn a universal conclusion with a minor premise because he has said that protection is necessary to save Canada: I have given protection to the industrialists, therefore I have saved Canada. I think that is fair oomment and I submit that was entirely the policy and program of the leader of the opposition during the whole of those five years. I suggest to my right hon. friend that he again pursue
the study of logic. He will find it useful in dealing with these matters.
The Prime Minister said that immediately on attaining office he would proceed to deal with the United States in connection with a trade treaty. He made no promises in his speeches, but the platform of the Liberal party did invoke wider markets for the people of this country. In fulfilment of the intimation that he would proceed to deal with the United States the Prime Minister met Mr. Armour, United States minister, the day after the present government was sworn in. During the election certain people were saying that there was no difference between the Liberal and the Conservative party. I think this is an illustration of the real difference between the two parties. We saw a former Prime Minister making promises which were not fulfilled, and we have the present Prime Minister fulfilling statements given during the campaign. The leader of the opposition went to Washington with the idea of arranging a treaty, but he did not and could not oomplete one. The Prime Minister went to Washington to arrange a trade treaty and he completed the arrangements. I know of no better illustration of the difference between Liberals and Conservatives in trade matters.
Sometimes you hear people say, "Just tweedledum and tweedledee," and when they utter these words they think that expresses everything, and they have proved their case. I hope the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) will read what I say. So far as this treaty is concerned, I am in hearty accord with its provisions. I realize that this is the first break that has been made in the crust of economic nationalism under which this and other countries of the world have been during the last five or six years. I realize that this is the first time an attempt has been made to show the world that a break can be made in this crust and I am proud that the Liberal party of Canada, through its Prime Minister, was able to make this break.
I listened to and read carefully the speeches of both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition and I found it extremely puzzling to discover the objections of the leader of the opposition to the terms of the treaty. I have endeavoured to put those objections under different headings and I believe I am fair in making this presentation. In the first- instance, he took about fifteen columns of Hansard to give a resume of the history of the Conservative Dartv with regard to tariff matters. I am bound to say that the Prime Minister also took a large number

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
of columns to outline the history of the Liberal party on the same matter. I do not quarrel with this because I believe the historian of the future will be anxious to know contemporary thought and both these speeches will be of value in days to come.
The leader of the apposition could hardly object to the time factor in the agreement. Such an objection had gone by the boards as a fixed time had been inserted in other agreements. He did say that in 1911 he objected to the reciprocity treaty because there was no fixed time limit, because either party could cancel the agreement almost at their own sweet will. As far as this treaty was concerned, he was bound by his own actions because he had signed treaties containing a time limit. The president of the United States was empowered to sign an agreement only for a period of three years. The leader of the opposition could not say very much about this feature of the agreement.
His next objection was to that hoary old sinner that is always resurrected, the adverse trade balance. I thought that particular theory had been exploded long ago. I thought it was agreed that an adverse trade balance with one particular country did not matter. That is the enlightened opinion, but the leader of the opposition seems to be an ardent believer in the old theory. Surely there is no doubt as to the fallacy of that argument. The error occurs in the belief that the debits and credits of countries are settled in the same way as are debits and credits of individuals who may buy and sell goods in one particular country. That is not the way in which the trade of countries is carried on; debits and credits are settled largely by bills drawn upon the debtor nations.
The next objection was that Canada had given a larger number of reductions than had the United States. This objection was fully and completely dealt with by the Minister of Finance this afternoon and no word of mine can add anything to what he said. There was also the favoured nation treatment provision. There cannot be any great objection to this as we have a similar clause in most of the agreements that have been consummated by Canada. We know the effect of such a provision; we know that it opens the door to Canada in many ways. The leader of the opposition knew that his hand was bound by the former treaties which had been signed by the government of which he was the head. He could not say much about that particular feature, but nevertheless that is one of the objections he took to this treaty.
He dealt also with the question of direct shipment and the injury that might be sus-
|Mr. Glen.]
tained by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific railway. Again this matter has been dealt with by the Minister of Finance and I need not deal with it further. In a forty minute speech it would be impossible to deal with all the objections taken, but there are one or two remarks of the leader of the opposition to which I wish to take objection. At the beginning of his speech he said that he did not suppose his hon. friends opposite would be prepared to concede to him the same degree of sincerity that they claimed for themselves. I think the right hon. gentleman is entirely in error in making a statement of that kind. I think he must admit that we of the west are sincere in the principles we advocate in this house. When the Prime Minister asked the leader of the opposition why he had not completed an agreement with the United States, he replied: Because I prefer my country to office and power. I think he will agree in his calmer moments that the inference to be drawn from such a statement is bound to be offensive to many of us in this section of the house. The inference is that we are here simply for office and power, and that we are prepared to do anything in order to attain that. I wish to think that was simply a remark made in the heat of debate, such as a man usually regrets later on, and as such I will regard it.
There are a number of hon. members here who by conviction and experience are free traders. When this treaty was brought before the house those of us of that type of mind were certainly in favour of it because we realized, as we have not been able to realize for some time, that the country has been given a hope of larger markets. This is one of the results of the policy of the Liberal party. We believe that is not the end of the tariff reform program of the Liberal party, and the country expects that it is not.
From the point of view of western Canada -and I say this without any desire to offend those of the east who are directly interested in industries, as distinct from farming-when we see, after the treaty has been invoked and promulgated, some of the implement industries of the east taking the position that despite the reduction of the duties they immediately increase the price of the articles they produce, we wonder just what they suppose that the country, after the election of October 14, will think of that attitude. Do those people think that the resources of statesmanship are exhaused in the mere winning of an election? Do they realize that their action has called forth condemnation throughout the whole of this dominion, and particularly in the west? When duties are reduced, an in-

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
crease in price does not seem logical, and I was glad to hear the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens) make in this connection the suggestion to the Prime Minister that some satisfaction should be given to the people as to why it was necessary to raise the price despite the fact that the duties had been decreased.
These parties in the east who think that industries alone have the right of control over their prices, and do not take into account the farmers of the west, who after labouring for forty or fifty years see their patrimony dissipated and disappearing daily, although the employment they give to the vast number of men engaged in agriculture is just as material to the interests of this country as is the business of the east, should realize that there must be a spirit of compromise in a country as diverse as ours and with such varied interests. Yet we find that just following the promulgation of the treaty, these prices are raised against the farmers. I say with all sincerity that I have never heard so many suggestions of division in the west as I did in the last election. The appeals that were being made and the utterances that were being given on the question of the division of this country were more pronounced than at any time I have known. When you get an instance such as we have in this case, that merely accentuates the situation. Vast numbers of people from all over the country are writing to the members complaining about the matter, and asking the reason. They demand that the Liberal government shall see to it that these manufacturers shall not impose their will upon us very long. I am therefore entirely in accord with what was said by the hon. member for East Kootenay that this is also a matter for investigation. If there is a proper answer, all right, let us have it; we want to know it, but certainly the people of Canada have a right to learn the explanation of these industries in raising their prices.
I should also like to point out, with every desire for unity between the different parts of the country, that both in the west and in the east there is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party who have not taken a position with regard to trade. They do not think the same way as I do in this respect. They are rather casual about trade. To them it is a matter of some importance but not of the importance that we give to it. I would point out that upon their attitude towards this agreement will depend to a large extent the success they will have in their appeal to the people. If they do not support, as I think they ought, an agreement which will tend to lighten the
burdens of the farmers throughout the west, they will certainly be faced with the response of the people that progress and prosperity are the negation of their party's hopes. I submit to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that in this they are dealing with realities, realities which have been reduced to concrete form. This is something which, judged in the light of history, must necessarily respond to the benefit of the common people. It is a reality reduced to concrete form. Are these representatives of the west and the east going to deny to the government of the day that support which is necesary to show not only to the United States but even further than that, across the water to the old land, that Canada is ready to trade with her neighbours, ready if necessary to give concessions freer than have ever before been given, and that we are ready to act as neighbours?
In connection with that, Mr. Speaker, there has been considerable discussion with regard to another agreement. The Prime Minister took the earliest possible moment to complete this agreement with the United States. I suggest that he is now in a position to treat with the old country. In the Ottawa agreements what I would call a savage bargain was made by Canada as against the old land. I refer particularly to section 11 of the Ottawa agreements providing for the equation of prices in costs of production as between Canada and Great Britain. I assert that it will be impossible for the parties to reach agreement on that question of prices with a view to the enlargement of trade between the two countries. An impossible barrier has been erected, a barrier which must be removed. I do not think I am asking the Prime Minister to do something in a hurry, but I do say that the Ottawa agreements, which do not expire until 1937, could very well be approached now.
My correspondence with persons in the old country and my reading of newspapers of the day lead me to the conclusion that old country people are ready, willing and anxious to meet the Prime Minister of Canada to-day and enter into agreements which will be satisfactory to both parties and not to one party alone. In the guarded statements of their statesmen after the last election here, one can read between the lines the expression of the relief they felt and the hope and expectation they have that Canada will come to them now and make a bargain that will be worth while. I am anxious to see that completed because I believe that the bonds of trade are stronger even than the bonds of blood, and that our trade with the United States, if it grows as much as we expect, may lead to a division between ourselves and the old land, which division can be avoided

Canada-XJ. S. Trade Agreement
now by a trade agreement satisfactory to both countries. I therefore suggest to the Prime Minister that it is not necessary to wait until 1937 before an approach is made. I am quite certain that the response he will receive from the old country will be such as to gladden the hearts of himself and his government and all the people of Canada. I therefore make that suggestion in all seriousness to the government. I hope it will be acted upon, and soon.
Do hon. members realize this fact also, that Britain is making treaties with other countries, and the time may come when she may say that she is not anxious to make treaties with Canada because we have shown in these Ottawa agreements that we are more concerned for our trade than we are in the kinship which it was thought existed between both countries. The day may come, and very early, when Britain may say that she is not anxious to treat on these matters; that she cannot and perhaps will not consider a trade bargain, although the Prime Minister of Canada more than any other man is in a position to make compromises in the matter of trade with the old land.
I am glad indeed to be able to say that this treaty has evoked a warm response in the- west. In fact it may have created hopes that cannot be fulfilled. The hon. member for East Kootenay said that this was not all that could be obtained; that the benefits we have secured would not rectify everything. Everyone realizes that fact, and in one of his radio addresses the Prime Minister pointed out what I think is a very evident truth, that before reform there must be recovery. I entirely agree with that statement; we must have recovery before we can have these reforms. We need not necessarily delay reforms, but our efforts will be futile unless we are able to say that we have recovered sufficiently to bring about reforms. I agree that we have within the dominion many problems which have to be solved, but the first one we have before us is this question of trade. I have gone through this agreement. I am not entirely satisfied with all its terms. I should like it to be much more comprehensive, but I am willing to accept it knowing that it marks the establishment of a principle which will do much to raise the hopes of the people in the Dominion of Canada. Therefore I will support it with my whole heart.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have paid close attention to the speeches delivered so far during this debate, in the hope that I might be able to get a clearer vision of all the implications contained in this agreement. An agreement

between Canada and the United States is a matter of such immensity that it is by no [DOT]means easy to gather all its implications. A bargain can be made easily between two people; an agreement can be made without difficulty between two countries, provided you are ready to give enough. This agreement touches so many branches of industry and is so spread over all the nine provinces, with all their divided industries, that it is by no means easy, study though you may, to ascertain fairly the implications it contains.
I listened particularly to the long speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when introducing the resolution. I listened to the historical part of that speech. I was more interested in the latter years, when he dealt with them, than with the earlier ones, because during eleven of those latter years I was a member of this house. The right hon. gentleman chided the late administration for not having made more progress than it did. He expressed extreme regret that he was not in power during those years, because if he had been in power there would have been manifest progress, and that in spite of the fact that in the nine years during which he was in power, there was no progress; in spite of the fact that on two occasions during those nine years the United States raised its tariff to such an extent that Canada's trade was grievously affected, and in spite of the fact that the right hon. gentleman's view as to the proper action of the Canadian government at that time was that it should do nothing which could be looked upon as being of a provocative nature.
Probably it would be more correct to point out that these negotiations would not have attained the progress they did attain had it not been for the fact that the United States realized that in this country there was a virile government whose intention it was to govern Canada for the benefit of the Canadian people, and particularly for the benefit of the Canadian worker. There is very little doubt. 1 think, that had it not been for that virile government that was in power during those five years we should not have had the empire trade agreements we now have. I think it is evident also that the United States took note of the existence of that government and of the fact that its policy was to link up the trade relations of the empire as a preliminary step towards the negotiation of trade agreements with other nations of the world. It is noticeable that it was not until June, 1934, two years after the Ottawa agreements were consummated, that for the first time in history the United States congress empowered the

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
president to make trade agreements, with certain restrictions on his actions. After that had been accomplished the preparatory work went on at a much faster pace and by last summer a sufficient quantity of facts and figures had been collected to make it possible for the spokesmen of the two countries, after they had digested those facts and figures, to approach each other with the idea of coming down to definite terms of negotiation.
As the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has pointed out to the house, he discovered and reported to his government that what the United States required Canada to give was, in his opinion, too great a price to pay, so it was not possible for that government to consummate an agreement. Then, not unnaturally, the matter was dropped during the period of the election campaign. Later as a result of, shall I say, an accident of electoral arithmetic, my right hon. friend opposite found himself in a position of power. He then hastened to Washington and, using the same facts and figures, came to the conclusion that it was possible for Canada to pay that price. Hence we have this agreement which we are now debating.
It will be noticed that Canada gives the United States one of three things: the intermediate tariff, the most favoured nation treatment modification of the intermediate tariff or the special schedules attached to the treaty. These apply particularly to the commodities we have to sell to the United States and those the United States have to sell to us. In the short time at my disposal I propose to deal with the effect of this treaty on the fruit and vegetable industry, which is the principle industry in the constituency of Yale. It does not appear to me that the treaty has much effect on the other industries carried on in that district. I do not think the treaty has much effect on the dairy industry as carried on there or on the mining industry, which has to do with coal and copper, gold and silver. I do not think it has much effect on the lumbering industry as carried on in those hills and valleys, for that industry is not on an export basis; it depends for its prosperity on the prosperity of the other industries in that district, principally the fruit and vegetable industry.
In considering tariff matters as they relate to fruits and vegetables I always think that there are two facts which should be kept prominently in mind. One is that these commodities are perishable; they must be sold when they are ready to go to market. That market must be in a receptive condition. If the market is not. ready for them they must be destroyed or stored, and storage is costly for it has to take care of cold and heat, and to preserve
humidity by the most perfect ventilation. And it is only for a comparatively short time that these perishable products can be stored. The other fact that must be kept in mind in discussing trade with the United States is that we are dealing with a country in which the time of maturity of these perishable products is several weeks in advance of ours, and when a certain commodity produced in Canada is ready to roll towards our markets it arrives in such markets at a time when the same variety produced in the United States has almost finished its marketing period. And United States distributors have never shown any lack of desire to get rid of their surplus products by sending them into a market other than their own country to relieve their own market of pressure, and naturally it is not a matter of concern to them what the price is in the Canadian market.
