That distributors in the United States are still of that opinion we have an excellent illustration in the markets of Great Britain in recent months. Last season the apple crop in Great Britain failed; it looked as if there would be a bare market, and the United States have been shipping into the markets of Great Britain hundreds of thousands of packages of excellent apples, good in quality, beautifully packed, exactly the same quality, exactly the same pack as our boxed apples produced in British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec. The result was that prices were driven so low that our producers received barely the cost of production. But those United States apples went into Great Britain over a tariff of 4s. 6d. a hundredweight, so that with our producers receiving barely the cost of production the United States producers have been receiving forty cents a box less than that. This illustrates the fact that the United States distributor does not mind losing money on a certain portion of his crop so long as he can prevent it from disturbing his own market and driving down the price for the rest of his crop.
I want to spend a minute or two in refreshing the memories of hon. members with regard to the changes that have taken place in the Canadian tariffs on these commodities in recent years. Twenty-nine years ago a Liberal government amended the customs tariff by inserting section 6, known as the dumping clause. Unfortunately they never used it. Fourteen years ago the Liberal government of which my right hon. friend was the leader amended the Customs Act by the insertion of a clause which enabled the Minister of Customs, as he was then called, to proclaim a value for duty which would enable the dumping clause to be used. Unfortunately he never used it. In 1926 a Conservative government,

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
being in power for a few months, promptly proclaimed values for duty, and for two shipping seasons the producer in Canada had the reasonable opportunities of his own market, and the consumer did not sulfer. In March, 1928, however, my right hon. friend decided, owing to pressure brought to bear upon him by his free trade supporters, that the orders in council must go. They were all cancelled. With them went the values for duty; no more use was made of the dumping clause, and for two seasons the Canadian producer had the utmost difficulty in marketing his produce in the Canadian market.
In 1930 the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) brought in his famous budget, the budget which was to win the victory for the Liberal party. In introducing his budget he explained to the house that the government had considered the application of seasonal dirties, but had come to the conclusion that seasonal duties were not suitable to Canadian conditions. I have never understood why seasonal duties would not be suitable to Canadian conditions. It is not a particularly new idea; sixty-five years ago the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association advocated their use. As far as I am aware they were never tried. But in 1930 the government did not propose to adopt them because they did not consider them suitable. Again pressure was brought to bear upon the minister by the free trade section of the Liberal party, and to our surprise, after the gruelling which the schedules in that tariff received when that budget finally emerged from the committee we found that seasonal duties had been introduced into it all down the line. Then came the general election and the change of government, and one of the first actions of the new government was to proclaim once more the values for duty, and to invoke the dumping clause. For five shipping seasons the producer in Canada had the reasonable opportunities of his own market, and certainly it cannot be said that the consumer suffered.
I want now to turn to a consideration of the items in the treaty which affect the fruit and vegetable growing industry. They will be found principally in the schedule attached to the treaty. It will be noticed that, to speak in general terms, the duty on vegetables has been reduced from thirty per cent to fifteen per cent and the duty on fruit from twenty to fifteen per cent. If they are left with only that amount of protection. I am afraid that the fruit growers and the vegetable growers in Canada will find themselves in a parlous position. But as far as ten fruits and fifteen vegetables are concerned the government have taken power to apply the dumping 
clause in a modified way. They have power to declare a value for duty and added duty which shall not exceed four-fifths of the minimum amount used in the years 1933, 1934 and
1935.	To my mind the question turns on this point, that although this power is provided in the treaty, if we remember the actions of a Liberal government composed to a certain extent of the gentlemen who hold ministerial positions to-day, a doubt must exist in the mind of the producer whether the government proposes to use this method of protection. If they use it the next question would be: Do they propose to use it to the full extent of their power? If they do so use it, do they propose to use it in time? For it is obvious that if Canadian produce rolls towards the Canadian market and arriving there finds that market cluttered up with the surplus of another country, and prices consequently very low, it will be of little assistance then to impose a value for duty, for it is most improbable that in face of Canadian production that price will rise. To my mind the whole question in considering the effects of this treaty upon the industry turns on that fact.
But there are three commodities which come in for less kindly treatment than do the others. There is one fruit, strawberries, and two vegetables, celery and lettuce, which receive considerably less assistance than do other fruits and vegetables. Why they have been selected for special treatment I do not know. As hon. members are aware strawberries are produced in considerable commercial quantities in British Columbia, Ontario and parts of Quebec. Just at the time when our strawberries are ready for the market they find themselves in a market cluttered up with the surplus of United States crops, which are just clearing up, and at a time when distributers in the United States are using every endeavour to keep that large quantity off their market. They do not care what happens to the Canadian market. Even though the minister employs to the greatest extent and at the proper time the powers provided in the treaty, strawberries will receive less protection than they did under the 1930 budget, without the assistance of any dumping duty. Similarly, in the Armstrong section of the Okanagan valley celery of quality is grown, and it is put up in such a pack that it is known throughout Canada. In California, just to the south of us, they do not grow their lettuce and celery by tens of acres; they grow it by thousands of acres, and it appears to me that British Columbia and Ontario will find themselves tremendously handicapped because of lack of assistance even to the extent of that

Canada-U. S. Trade Agreement
contained in the 1930 budget, to say nothing of the help producers of those two commodities have been receiving in the last five years.
Last year Canada imported $2,500,000 worth of vegetables and $2,500,000 worth of fruits, principally from the United States, of kinds and varieties produced in Canada. In the fiscal year 1929-30 we imported a little more than $7,000,000 worth of fruits and $8,000,000 worth of vegetables. Conditions in 1929-30 were very different from conditions obtaining to-day, and it does not seem at all improbable that the amount Canada will import in coming years under the provisions of this treaty will very considerably increase. I know of no variety of fruit or vegetable produced in Canada which could not be produced to a point which would go a very long way towards supplying the needs of the Canadian consumer at the time he requires them, namely in the actual producing season.
An examination of the effects of this treaty on commodities other than those mentioned in the special schedule reveals the fact that there are two which in future will come in under the intermediate tariff. I am referring to cut flowers and potatoes. Hitherto cut flowers came in from the United States under a tariff of forty per cent and potatoes under one of seventy-five cents a hundred. In future both will come in free. On Canadian soil and under Canadian conditions there is no question that dotted across Canada flowers of excellence are being grown. There are many occasions in our lives when we wish to purchase flowers; usually we want them in a hurry and are particularly anxious to get them. It seems to me most unlikely that florists will be able to produce in anything like the same volume they have produced in the past if in the future cut flowers come in free of duty from the United States, where frequently they are grown with the assistance of cheap labour, and, if they be hothouse production, under lower fuel costs prevailing in the United States.
It is less easy to understand the situation produced by the treaty with regard to potatoes, because in connection with this commodity Canada is on an export basis. Last year she exported five times as much as she imported. Surely the government does not propose to balance the trade in potatoes. Surely it is unlikely that the United States will fail to make use of the situation described by the Prime Minister in these words:
Of the other products not covered by the trade agreement the most important are codfish and table potatoes, and in the case of both these products low prices and depressed
conditions in the industries concerned in the United States made it impossible for the government of that country to consider the granting of concessions on these products at the present time.
I do not know if that can properly be connected with what I am referring to, but it amounts to this, that the price is so low in the United States that we will now let them enter Canada free, while Canada is on an export basis. However the government, if the minister sees fit, can correct these difficulties. He has pointed out, and quite correctly, that it is quite impossible for him to reveal the secrets of the budget before its introduction. I find myself in the position of having to endeavour to judge the treaty on the facts which present themselves to me at this time. Whereas these two commodities used to come in here under a tariff they now come in free, and I do not see how the producers can be other than troubled and anxious with regard to possible results.
For a few moments I should like to look at the other side of the treaty, and see what Canada receives. I find that in the future apples may enter the United States under a duty of fifteen cents a bushel rather than one of twenty-five cents. I wonder if hon. members know that forty-one states of the union produce apples on a commercial scale. I wonder if they have considered whether in view of that fact it is probable that Canada will be able greatly to increase the $10,000 worth of apples she sent to the United States last year. It does not seem to me that a country which grows apples to the enormous extent they are grown in the United States, and which has a proclivity for dumping its produce on our markets, will be very receptive to an increase in the supply of apples from Canada.
The duty on strawberries is reduced from one and one-quarter cents per pound to three-quarters of a cent per pound. Last year we exported $19,000 worth to the United States. I have already pointed out that when our strawberries are ready to move to the market they come up against the tail end of the United States strawberry season. Is it likely, then, that we shall find a receptive market in the United States for our strawberries? The duty on cherries is cut in half. We exported so small a quantity last year and in recent preceding years that they are not even mentioned separately, but come in under the heading of other fruits, n.o.p.
The duty on peas is cut in half for three months. There, again, the amount which we have shipped is negligible. Then we come back to potatoes. The duty on potatoes has

Canada-ZJ. S. Trade Agreement
been reduced for certain months and a quota established. They want to buy our seed grain from this northern climate, but as we are on an export basis already, as they are allowed to ship their potatoes into Canada free, as our producers of early potatoes have more than enough to supply the Canadian market, it is very questionable to my mind whether we shall benefit greatly from that item.
The tariff on turnips is cut in half, and I think that will help. Two areas in Canada produce turnips on a commercial basis, and we shipped into the United States last year $396,000 worth. It may be that other areas in Canada will be able to turn to the production of turnips and that this reduction in the tariff will assist us.
The tariff on cabbage is reduced from two to 1J cents. The quantity we shipped last year was negligible, but the quantity which the United States shipped to us last year was $161,000 worth, and four years ago it amounted to $450,000 worth. I do not think it is very probable that we shall get much assistance on cabbage.
So here we have seven items in the fruit and vegetable schedules on which we do get tariff assistance of a sort from the United States, but the whole of the rest of the fruits and vegetables which we produce will remain under the Hawley-Smoot tariff. In endeavouring to come to a fair decision with regard to the implications of this treaty regarding advantages to this particular industry, I am bound to say that I cannot find any. But the whole matter, let me emphasize, turns on the willingness or otherwise of the Minister of Finance to make use of the powers under his hand, and I would remind him once more that although the amount he can use is less than it was-I must also refer to the fact that it is a method of protection against which he set his face in an adamant way in 1930-the harm which this treaty may do to the fruit and vegetable industry will be considerably lessened if he will use that power to the full, and if he will use it in time.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT PROPOSED APPROVAL SUBJECT TO LEGISLATION MAKING PROVISIONS EFFECTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this debate adjourns and the house goes into committee I should like to say that it has been a source of satisfaction to me to have occupied a grandstand seat in the House of Commons while the two old stalwart political parties have been riding the hobby-horse of high versus low tariffs around the racecourse on its perennial run which it has been following now since 1867. It has been quite enlightening to watch it.

I should like to refer to a remark that was made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) last night when he said, "My hon. friends in the far comer who say that the people of western Canada are not interested in trade are lucky that they do not have to go back to the country very soon." I wish to correct any misunderstanding that hon. members may 'have in thinking that we in this comer are not interested in trade. I do not wish those words to be put into our mouths at all. We, in western Canada are very greatly interested in trade, and we here in this corner representing Alberta are vitally interested in trade. We feel, however, that our interest is more in internal trade than in external trade at this time. We do not believe with the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that external trade is going to solve the problem which now confronts Canada and do away with our unemployment problem and our relief camps and the various other troubles that confront us. We have no real hope that this trade treaty which is now being completed with the United States will bring back any very great measure of prosperity.
We have no really fundamental fault to find with the treaty, and I myself am going to vote for the passage of this resolution now being debated, but I am doing so not with any pious prayer that this new agreement, which might have been efficacious many years ago in the history of Canada, is going to be the one panacea we have needed these last five years to put our unemployed to work and that sort of thing. Our interest is in trade, in free trade, in lots of trade, but we might well have spent the time we have taken on this debate, and perhaps more,, and I hope we shall before parliament prorogues, in devising ways and means whereby trade ihside Canada might be stimulated so that our own citizens might be provided with the means for consuming to the full. Then, after that, we might make agreements with foreign countries for the disposal of our surplus. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall spend just as much time on this new horse, which is not a wooden one like the hobby-horse of high versus low tariffs, and so, not being wooden, is likely eventually to arrive somewhere.
I have a. particular interest in the last paragraph of the communication which passed between the Canadian legation in Washington and the Hon. Cordell Hull, Secretary of State of the United States, and signed by

Supply-National Revenue
H. H. Wrong. Charge d'Affaires. The last paragraph reads as follows:
I am further directed to state that the Canadian government propose to invite parliament to permit the entry free of duty and charges of incidental purchases by residents of Canada returning from the United States of America, not exceeding the value of one hundred dollars, under regulations, particularly as to the frequency of such entry and duration of visits, to be prescribed, for such time as treatment substantially equivalent to that now in effect is accorded by the government of the United States of America to incidental purchases by residents of that country returning from Canada.
People meet in tourist camps; travellers meet on the trains and in many instances the conversation turns to the great difference in the treatment regarding the entry of purchases accorded to American and Canadian tourists. Sometimes the American tourists feel a certain superiority which we do not like. My constituency of Medicine Hat touches on the international boundary. Many of my constituents live long distances from the stores and populated centres in Canada and they find it more convenient to cross the boundary to the towns of Montana. On their behalf I feel very grateful that it will be possible for them to avoid the temptations which are always in the way of such people to smuggle ordinary articles into Canada. I am glad to know that travellers and tourists going into the United States will be able to bring back those little articles which they feel they want and which they [DOT] feel can be bought more advantageously in that country. They will not then be tempted to smuggle these articles into Canada. As a guide to what I expect from this government, I will read a paragraph from the United States Tariff Act of 1930. This is paragraph 1798 of the act, and it reads:
Residents of the United States returning from abroad' are allowed $100 in value on articles acquired by them for personal and household use or as souvenirs or curios. These articles can be brought in free of duty provided they are not bought on commission or intended for sale; provided, that a resident of the United States shall not take advantage of the exemption herein granted within a neriod of thirty days from the last exemption claimed.
The last paragraph of Mr. Wrong's letter reads in part as follows:
-for such time as treatment substantially equivalent to that now in effect is accorded by the government of the United States of America to incidental purchases by residents of that country returning from Canada.
There is no definition there of a tourist or there is no stipulation as to how long one must remain in a foreign country before he is allowed this privilege. The real teeth in
the United States act are that a returning resident must not use the privilege more than once every thirty days, and that the goods must not be bought on commission or intended for sale. It is my hope that the Canadian regulation will be similar to the American one and not specify a certain period which a tourist must remain in a country before he can take advantage of this exemption. Newspaper articles have appeared from time to time indicating that this period will be all the way from three weeks to three months. I hope the regulations will not be so couched that they will remove entirely the benefit of that particular clause.
On motion of Mr. Leader the debate was adjourned.

The house in committee of supply, Mr, Sanderson in the chair.
Salaries, $946,240; contingencies, $75,000.
Will the minister give the committee particulars of the increases in this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: The increase of $74,910 in salaries is due to statutory increases and the transfer of about forty-five clerks from the temporary to the permanent staff and the establishment of ten additional positions of a minor character. The decrease in the contingencies of $22,700 is accounted for by the transfer of the forty-five officials mentioned already. The amount involved in this change is approximately $45,000, but from this amount must be subtracted an increase of $15,300 in the appropriation for printing and stationery to provide for tabulating equipment in the statistical branch, and an increase of $7,000 in sundry expenditures to provide for travelling expenses of officers of the headquarters staff.

Before this administration came into office consideration was given to coordinating the preparation of statistical information, and the mention of the tabulating equipment brings this fact to my mind. Could the minister advise us if anything has been done in this direction? The minister knows, perhaps better than I, that at the end of each month his department endeavours to get out with great rapidity information in connection with the trade during the month. A certain amount of tabulation also takes place in the statistical branch of the Depart-
Supply-National Revenue

ment of Trade and Commerce. An. effort was being made to see whether something could not be done to coordinate this and prevent duplication of effort and expenditures

We are working on that all the time. The method of tabulation now employed in the Department of National Revenue has been worked out with Doctor Coats of the bureau of statistics. That is about all the information I think I can give.

I should like to draw a little incident to the attention of the committee and the minister. Although it is not very important, it may be symptomatic of many incidents which take place on our border line affecting people who return from the United States. A week ago yesterday I was crossing the border from Ogdensburg to Prescott and I was asked at the boundary if I had anything to declare. It so happened that I had in my possession a small box of cigars which had been given me and wliich I declared to the customs official there; it contained twenty-three cigars. I do not smoke, but I brought them back-at least I thought I was going to bring them back-for some friends in the house who do smoke. I told the customs official that I had there a box of cigars valued at, I think, exactly SI.10. He figured out what the duty would be and said it would be exactly $2.40 for cigars which cost retail SI.10. I told him he had better keep the cigars there and we would see what could be done about a duty of eleven cents on a cigar which cost a nickel retail on the other side. I asked for a receipt, which was given me. What I was wondering was: What is the disposition of goods that are impounded or retained by customs officials? I was told that these cigars would go up in smoke, but whether they were burnt or not I cannot say. I was told, however, by officials of the department that goods which are detained or seized by customs officials are destroyed by them at certain stated periods.
Destroyed by smoking.

It seems to me that if such is the case it is a most absurd regulation that anything which is seized or is left behind with customs officials should be destroyed, when there are many places where real use could be made of those articles. For instance, in the case of whiskey or cigars which happen to be seized by customs officials, it would strain my imagination a good deal to believe that all those goods are destroyed. I can hardly imagine that our officials are so honourable and generous that they can allow them-

selves to see good smokes and good whiskey going to waste in that way. I hardly think they would take the whiskey and pour it into the river St. Lawrence, nor do I think they would dispose of cigars in that way. But I do think, Mr. Chairman, that as regards goods seized or left at customs houses there should be some definite means of knowing what is done by way of disposing of them. In the case of such articles as I have just mentioned I see no reason in the world why, for instance, the tobacco could not go to some old folks home in the neighbourhood, and the liquor to the hospitals. I think it is ridiculous to waste material of which good use could be made. I have mentioned this matter privately to the minister. I should like him to inform the committee, if he can, how much goods have really been destroyed over a period of time and the character of the goods that have been so wasted.

I think it will be possible to get the information for my hon. friend. The regulations are very strict as to the destruction of that class of goods, they are destroyed periodically when the inspectors visit the customs houses in question. I do not think, from information I have had since being in the department, that the suspicions of my hon. friend are justified, because nothing is more strict than the insistence upon the destruction of goods that are seized under such circumstances as he has mentioned.
But is there any reason in the world why these goods should be destroyed at all?

I have not given consideration to the policy underlying the provisions of the act, but that is the law. I suppose, if it were mot, abuses would creep in. One would have to be very careful about the destination of seized goods.
Is it the law or is it a regulation under the law that these goods have to be destroyed?
It is the law.

Does the minister not think that, in cases such as those to which I have just referred, the law might very well be altered and that we should stop the wasteful destruction of goods which might be serviceable to people in this country who need them?
I shall be very glad to give consideration to my hon. friend's suggestion. It would, however, require amendments to both the Customs Act and the Excise Act.

Let us have them.

Supply-National Revenue

On page 90 details are given of increases in several of the salaries. I assume these are the details of the item under discussion. I notice that the salary of the assistant commissioner of excise is increased by $300; that of the dominion customs appraiser is also increased. Are those statutory increases under the Civil Service Act or are they matters within the discretion of the minister under the National Revenue Act?
Both are statutory increases.
Does that apply to the whole list set out on pages 90 and 91?
In the main, yes.

I want to ask the minister one question and see if I caught his answer correctly. There is an increase of fifty-five persons in the service of the department, from 474 to 529. In reality, I gathered from what the minister said, there was a very slight increase, forty-five being already there, who show now where they were not shown before.
That is correct. The forty-five were taken from the temporary classification and put in the permanent classification.
When was that?
A few months ago.
Before or since this government came in?
Before the change of government.
That is what I thought.
I notice an item, examiner of publications and director of publicity, $4,200. Can the minister explain to the committee the duties and functions of the gentleman who occupies that position?

That official is charged with the administration of the tariff item which prohibits the entry of certain literature, which is seditious, immoral and so forth. That is one of his duties. He has others as well.

That was the item of which I was thinking. I observe that the gentleman in question has vested in him very wide powers, and of a kind which I do not think he ought to have. Under his jurisdiction, his guidance, literature which ought to come into this country is often banned. Literature that we can find in practically all our public libraries is not allowed into Canada. I do not know what special qualifications the official in question has for saying what literature should and what literature should not come into this country. But I do think matters of this kind,
concerning what is fit for people to read, or what publications should be allowed entry into Canada, should not come under the Department of National Revenue at all. They ought to be under some department more competent, I believe, to judge of these questions than is the department which is charged with the collection of the revenues of this dominion.
I have had a little experience with this department in the past in reference to the banning of books. I remember that I went to a former minister of this department and asked if he thought certain books ought to be banned. He told me that he did not think so, but in the meantime the official of the department had banned those books which the minister thought ought to be allowed free entry into this country. I want to know what authority is given this gentleman in question; how he judges what books are to be banned and how he comes to exercise the authority and jurisdiction which he does exercise.

Someone has to do it, Mr. Chairman. Really it is the minister who bans the books, but of course the minister cannot read all the books, so we have to get the most competent official possible to examine this literature. With regard to the qualifications of Mr. Roe, I may say that he is a journalist of many years standing and a former member of the press gallery, with a long record of public service. I have no reason to think his qualifications are not of the highest character. I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he has in mind any particular books that were banned which in his opinion should have been admitted.

I was referring to ordinary
books of a socialistic character that, to my own knowledge, have been banned, books that were published by Charles Kerr and Sons, of Chicago, that were held up by the department and not allowed to come into Canada.

Would the hon. gentleman
give me the name of the book or books by the author he has named, which literature he thinks should have been admitted?

The name I mentioned is
that of a publishing house in Chicago which publishes a more radical type of literature. My colleague from Vancouver East tells me that he can give an instance.

I had a letter a day or two ago with regard to a book that to my knowledge has been in circulation in British Columbia for the last twenty years. The title is Socialism, Utopian and Scientific, by Friederioh Engels. As a matter of fact it is
Supply-National Revenue

an old classic that has been in circulation for the last thirty-five years. Why it should be held up now is something beyond my comprehension.
I will look into the matter.

If the minister will not
mind I should like to say that a great many complaints were received, even by myself, that we were entirely too lenient in our administration in this regard. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) could be quite easily satisfied as to why this comes under the customs department. There is in our customs tariff an item which has been there for many years, forbidding the importation into our country of immoral or salacious literature, or literature that promotes revolution-I will put it in that way-or the use of force for the attainment of political ends. Someone has to determine whether a given book is immoral or salacious or whether it advocates the accomplishment of purposes in the manner I have indicated. There have been frequent complaints received to my knowledge, in fact by myself personally, with regard to books dealing with what one might call the new economic theories that advocate the accomplishment of a complete change in our social system by methods that at least the Supreme Court of Ontario have held to be improper. After that decision books that at times had come in freely were confiscated, because they constituted a violation of the provisions of the statute in the light of the decision that was given.

The book mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East is looked upon as a classic the world over. I assume one could find it in the public library here, though I have never tried to do so. I have no doubt it is in the parliamentary library; I believe if I sent for it I would get it. But, while it is permitted in all our public libraries, if anyone sends to the United States for a copy of the same book it will be held up and confiscated and considered to come within the classification of banned literature. I realize that there may be some force in the argument of the leader of the opposition, but there is the difficulty of allowing one individual to say what literature should be permitted to come through the customs and what should not be permitted to come through.
I think perhaps there is more involved in this than appears on the surface. It may be true that in some cases communications have come to the department urging that they should be a little stricter in their application of the ban on certain types of works, perhaps of a radical, socialistic or communistic character.

On the other hand, we might ask for a ban on all fascist or nazi literature, and so on. One cannot say one form of literature must be banned while another of similar type is allowed entry. I think the gentleman in question, under whose jurisdiction lies this very important question of saying what is fit to read and what is not fit to read, should be guided by some definite policy, and there should be uniformity so far as the actions of the department are concerned.

I would not like the hon. gentleman to go away with the idea that the department, the minister or any official has the right, by law, to determine what people may or may not read generally. All the department can do is administer a certain item of the tariff. That is item 1201 of schedule C of the tariff:
Prohibited goods:	Books, printed paper,
drawings, paintings, prints, photographs or representations of any kind of a treasonable or seditious, or of an immoral or indecent character.
Necessarily there must be some discretion in deciding what is of a treasonable or seditious or an immoral or indecent character. To tell the truth, I do not know how the difficulty can be overcome. I will look into the question of the book mentioned by my hon. friend. I do not know its status, at the moment; that is, whether or not it has been banned.

I should like to direct attention to a procedure which causes some inconvenience and hardship to booksellers. I refer to that class of literature which cannot be regarded as treasonable or seditious, and which has been in more or less general circulation in Great Britain and the United States. In the past the practice has been to hold up these books at ports of entry in British Columbia and other provinces and send them to Ottawa for examination. If it is. found ultimately that they are not on the banned list, they are allowed to enter. Possibly in some cases some over-zealous officials have held up books in this way. I should like to suggest that some procedure be found which will do away with this hardship to the booksellers and avoid this inconvenience to those who have ordered books and who believe they are entitled to receive them. May I ask as to the policy in that regard?

There are very few complaints of any hardship resulting from this practice. If the hon. gentleman would suggest any other procedure which might be followed I should certainly be glad to give the matter consideration, I presume there are occasions

Supply-National Revenue
when the collector does not feel himself qualified to decide whether the book is of a character to bring it under the item, and so he forwards it to the department for examination.
And to secure uniformity.
Yes.

I have had from time to time a number of complaints about the holding up of certain papers and books which I find on inquiry are not banned. Only a few days ago I had an inquiry from a prominent citizen of Alberta with regard to the Moscow News, which is not a propagandist organ, strictly speaking, but is a news organ printed in English. I remember some years ago on returning from two or three weeks in Russia I subscribed to that paper just to know what was going on. I subscribed for it in London, England, at a regular bookshop. My copy came through regularly. After the year expired I did not renew my subscription. But now I have a number of protests from different parts of the country, people saying that although they had subscribed through the London office they had difficulty in getting their paper. Only a few days ago I had a similar protest from Alberta about the paper not coming through. I understand it is not on the banned list. Why it should be held- up at some local post office or by some customs official in the west, I cannot imagine. Can the minister give us some idea as to the mode of procedure in the matter?

I think perhaps some collector might detain the Moscow News, not knowing, and wishing to ascertain, whether it is properly admissible. I believe, however, that such occurrences as the hon. member mentions are very rare; very little complaint has been made to the department of anything of that character.

I said it was quite possible that that book which was banned might be found in the parliamentary library. I have just sent a page for the -book called Socialism, Utopian and Scientific, and from the parliamentary library comes this book that has been banned by the minister's officials. It has been in print since 1892. I do not have to comment on this matter any further; it shows the absurdity of some of the regulations put into effect by the individual in question. In spite of whatever qualifications he may have I think he must be governed by certain considerations that prompt him to ban books which can be found in practically every library in Canada, public, university, and private.
I must find out whether that particular book is banned or not. I should be very much surprised to find that it is.

A rather serious instance occurred recently in Toronto. A man named John Stimak was fined $100 for having in his possession some Lenin books. On questioning Mr. Roe, the official referred to, he made the statement to me and my colleague on the right (Mr. MacNeil-) that he endeavoured always to permit such books to come into Canada if they were philosophic in character and not definitely propagandist, but that his action did not affect the Stimak case; that once the book is in the country it remains for the various provinces to decide whether they shall permit it to be handled by their citizens. That seems a very ridiculous state of affairs. If the book is permitted to enter Canada it should be permitted to enter every province, and if a man in good faith is importing books that are permitted by the dominion customs to enter, then there should be no penalty for being in possession of those books in any province of the dominion.
This also should be said, that when a minister is considering the banning of books that advocates the use of force to change the social system he should also bear in mind the banning of books that advocate force to maintain the social system, and there are plenty of such books in circulation at the present time.
The seventh item on page 90 provides for an assistant private secretary, apparently the creation of a new position. Is that an assistant private secretary to the minister?
Yes.

Further down there is another item:	secretaries to executive.
Apparently last year one executive had a secretary, and for the following year two are to have them. To which executive of the department is a secretary -being provided that was not being previously provided?

One of these positions was previously in existence and is in the office of the commissioner of excise. The other one is not filled. It provides for a position in the minister's office, and there is no present intention of filling it.
Then why include it in the estimates?
Well, it makes provision.

But if it is not necessary and there is no intention to fill it, why provide



Supply-National Revenue
money for it? Judging by the minister s answer it is not a provision for a secretary for some executive in the department; apparently it is a provision for a secretary in the minister's office in addition to the private secretary who has always been there, and an assistant private secretary, which position is also provided for by these estimates.

That is correct. The
provision is made to give some little latitude in the organization of the minister's office. There is no secretary to an executive there other than the assistant private secretary, and there is no present intention of putting one there. But this gives a little latitude in case it should be necessary.

In other words provision is being made in these estimates for an assistant private secretary to the minister, an official he did not previously have, and for another secretary to the minister under the title of secretary to executive. Surely that cannot be so.
I am informed that there was an assistant private secretary before.
For a time, yes.

Then why
complain now?

I am not complaining; I am asking for information. I have not made the slightest complaint, but when I see in the estimates an item which provides for a secretary to an executive, and the minister intimates that it is to be another secretary to the minister, obviously I think there must be something unusual in the situation, and I am trying to find out what it is. I supposed the executives in the national revenue department would be the commissioner of customs for example, the commissioner of excise, the commissioner of income tax. All I want to have clear is: Does this provision for an additional secretary as secretary to executive mean an additional secretary or assistant secretary to the minister?
There is and has been for many years provision for a secretary to the executive in nearly every minister's office.
For one, yes, and there has been one in the office of the Minister of National Revenue. But the minister is now providing for two.

No, only one secretary to executive. It is true that provision has been made for an assistant private secretary; that has been done there too. The only point is that I do not intend to fill that position.
[Mr. Li*\vsou.l
Mr. LAWSON; I hope the minister and I are not at cross purposes. He says that there is only one, but if he will read the item in the estimates he will find there is provision for two secretaries at $2,100, and that it is carried out to $4,200.
One is not in my office.
That is what I am trying to find out.
I thought I said that one is in the office of the commissioner of excise. The other is provided for, but as I say, I have no present intention of filling the position.
Carried.

Some hon. members must wish to hold up the estimates; if they do I promise the committee we could spend a long time on them. In connection with one or two items I see reductions in salaries without corresponding reductions in the number of employees. About half way down the page I find an item with reference to chemists. There were four in 1935-36 and provision is being made for the same number in these estimates, but there is a reduction of $200 in salaries to be paid. Then, further down the page the minister will find a reduction of $400 in salaries to assistant chemists, although the same number are being retained. I should like to know the reason for the reductions in the aggregate amounts paid.
The reason is that with the retirement of officials who have reached the age of sixty-five years-
Young men come in at lower grades.

-other men come in at
lower salaries.
May I revert to the banning of certain books. Perhaps the minister would give the committee a list of publications banned by his department.
I would be reluctant to do that, because to begin with it would be advertising salacious literature.

I do not wish to do that. The minister knows what I have in mind. I am thinking particularly of works along lines I discussed a few moments ago, and I think particularly of a book by Friederich Engels entitled Socialism, Utopian and Scientific. There must be many other works of the same type which have been banned by the department. A minute ago the minister wanted to know if there was a ban on the book. It is quite possible that so far as the

Supply-Fisheries
department is concerned there may be no official ban, but I do know that in certain parts of the country books are not allowed to go through the customs department.
The hon. member for Vancouver East has in his possession a communication from an organization in Vancouver asking him to inquire about the ban on this particular book. Evidently a ban must be exercised by some of the customs officials in certain parts of the country. I do not want any advertising of salacious literature in this house or anywhere else, but it is quite another matter when departmental officials attempt to bar from proper circulation books of a philosophical nature in which are discussed questions and which any person might read to good advantage. I am suggesting that the minister might read the book by Friederich Engels; it would not do him any harm, and it might do good to some other hon. members in the committee if they were to read it. The book in question was published forty or fifty years ago, and I believe if we had a list of banned literature it might help some of us who occasionally read books of that kind.

Despite the possible bad
effect produced by advertising books of a certain type, nevertheless I think we ought to have some indication of what books are banned. It is possible that these books are banned only to some people, and that other people may bring them in or get them. That would be an undesirable state of affairs. I have been informed that although certain literature was banned to some people, other people could get those books. When we speak about salacious literature we are talking about something altogether different. It should not be difficult to find out the books which would come under that heading. At the moment I am not prepared to say that it would be worth while to have a censor. We could not do anything for those who would be detrimentally affected by reading such books, and those who would not be affected would not be reading them. There is no reason in the world, however, why we should not have a list of books such as I have indicated, and we should know why they are or are not admitted into the country.

Would the minister accept a suggestion whereby the department would be approached by publishing houses and booksellers, listing with the department books of a philosophical nature read generally throughout the world? After they have been scrutinized by the department orders could be issued to the officers at the different ports of entry advising them that there would be no reason for banning such literature. I believe

is being done now.
I see an expenditure indicated for the salary of an expert tea tester. Is that an all year round job? I notice the salary is reduced by about $500.
It is an all year round job, beginning at the lower range. That is the reason for the reduction.

Fisheries-Salaries and contingencies, $133,331.
Is the salary of Mr. Larabee in this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext: Not in this item. He is a temporary employee.

There are a number of items I should like to discuss, but the list is so comprehensive that it is difficult to know which one to speak about. Speaking generally about the salary estimates I should like to suggest to the minister, who of course is new in his department, that what is badly needed in the department is a complete shake-up, and that applies both to officers at Ottawa, and particularly in British Columbia. In saying that I am not reflecting upon the management of the present minister or, indeed, upon that of his predecessor. The last minister was a victim, shall I say, and the present minister is liable to be embarrassed by the subtle, feather bed influence of his officials. They do not say to him: You shall not do so and so. That would possibly excite his suspicion and his resistance. But the continual dropping of water wears away the stone, and they yes, yes him, and then gently but quietly, day by day, influences are brought to bear and facts or semi-facts brought forward, and presently the minister finds himself committed to the stagnation of bureaucracy, than which there can be no more hopeless condition.
I do not suggest, when I say that there should be a shake up, that the minister should discharge the officials or attaches appointed by the late Conservative government, who have now become to a very large extent barnacles on the ship of state, and supplant them by Liberal attaches who in time would also become barnacles, but I use the word as I intend it; I mean: Shake them up. A certain section of the employees are
Supply-Fisheries

more or less asleep. Another section is composed of political hacks in every sense of the word. Another section, the larger one, and the most fatal of all, the one of which I, perhaps, complain most, is composed of those who have got into the official rut, and there is nothing more hopeless to get action from than that.
I have some knowledge of that situation myself, having been a civil servant for ten years, and I saw both in my own experience and that of others how the continued officials come to resent anyone coming forward with any suggestion that might mean action or change. We got into the position where we knew that it meant trouble and worry, and possibly a reprimand from the government for taking the wrong way instead of the right way. It was so much easier to make some general evasive reply or objection, and stall off the man or woman who wanted change. I was once told by a deputy minister of an important portfolio in this government, speaking from a long experience, "Mr. Neill, I get along best when I do nothing." He was deputy minister of an important department, and there are parts of this country suffering to-day from the policy or lack of policy indicated by his attitude. He is no longer a deputy, so I am not hurting anybody's feelings.
When I say, shake them up, I mean that those who have got into a more or less sleepy condition should be advised to wake up. The political hacks to whom I have referred, who got their positions through political influence- and I have no objection to that provided they carry out their duties-do not seem to be aware that there has been a change of government, and they are still continuing to play politics. I am referring more to British Columbia than to the offices here where, in fact, I know of none of that.
The third thing is to get them out of the rut, so that when a suggestion is made by people whose livelihood is at stake they will not simply sit down and write a letter, take the line apparently of least resistance, stall the man off, give him some form letter-I have received scores of them and have a dozen in front of me now-hoping that he will forget about the matter or give it up in despair.
Coming to the estimates themselves, I see the details are given on page 77. We know, if not from personal knowledge, at least from the press, that the government has told the different departments that they must cut down and practise economy. I do not know if they have been told that they must cut down their estimates to those of a certain year, or that a certain percentage must be cut off, or a certain sum, such as $200,000 or $300,000 must be cut

off. At any rate, glancing at this book of estimates, the result is obvious. Orders have been given-and I am not complaining of this -to cut down expenses. It is the method I wish to protest against, and it is perhaps not the fault of the officials so much as of the system that has been adopted.
The minister or his deputy is told, we will say, that he has to cut down to the amount of $200,000. There are only one or two ways in which he can do this. The deputy can either cut down his staff, dismiss some of them, or cut down the seasonal work that is done in the field. Why can he not cut down the salaries of his employees? He cannot do that because that is regulated by the government in another way. If the government wish to cut down the salaries of the civil service they do so, as they have done, by a blanket reduction all round, but that is not within the scope of the deputy or the minister who is told to cut down the expenses of his department.
Then the deputy is confronted with this situation: I have to cut down $200,000; I cannot take it off salaries; what am I going to do? One thing would be to reduce the staff, but did one ever hear of a deputy doing that? What is the whole idea of a man when he gets into public office but to build a bureau around himself. Give a man the job of shovelling snow between the east and the west block, and then go away and come back in ten years, and you would not find him shovelling snow any more; he would be the deputy superintendent general of snow shovelling, with an office of his own and a deputy and assistant deputy, an accountant, and probably a purchasing agent, and we would be mighty lucky if he did not have a publicity agent as well. The deputy cannot get away from the temptation of building a staff around himself, and the superintendent general of snow shovelling would, of course, get a bigger salary than the man handling the shovel. Very well then. The deputy is not going to cut down his staff for that reason; then there is also the pressure of friends, and all his subordinates have friends and relations who will put pressure upon him.
Then what is he going to do? He will do as we see revealed in the estimates. He will cut down on the practical work. Instead of cutting down these salaries I note that there is an increase of $4,893, practically $5,000 of an increase, mark you, in salaries. Then if you will look at page 44 you will find that substantial reductions are being made in the work that is carried on. There is a total reduction of $185,112 in the various items, and where did the bulk of that reduction come

Supply-Fisheries
from? The biggest item of salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol, and fisheries protection services. a very essential service in connection with the conservation of fish, is being cut down by $141,548 out of a total reduction of $185,112, while the overhead, the permanent salaries, has been increased by nearly $5,000. There are other items, some of which are being reduced thirteen per cent, some seventy-six per cent-that is one of the most important items that I shall deal with presently if I have time-another one, thirty-four per cent, and so on, while the overhead has been increased four per cent.
Partly it is the system that is wrong, and partly this is due to human nature; they do not like to go at it in the right way. It is inimical to the best interests of any industry, when economy and curtailment must be practised, that it should be practised on the practical work in the field rather than on the overhead. It might be said that the men working in the fields are also getting salaries, but they are cut out because they are seasonal men. The order goes out that instead of 150 guardians there shall be only eighty. Do hon. members realize the damage done by such a reduction? Streams that have been protected for fifteen years are left without guardians, and when a stream is left without guardians it means that poaching occurs, human nature being what it is. In British Columbia these conditions are particularly bad. There is an over-staffed office in Vancouver, but there is no suggestion of cutting down there. The really practical work in the field is to be curtailed.
Turning to the head office, I find that one man who is drawing a very substantial salary died but his position was filled at once. I believe his work could have been done by others in the department and there would have been an opportunity for some retrenchment. Instead of this, I notice that the staff at Ottawa has been increased from sixty to sixty-one. Then I notice a fisheries engineer, but that is all right. Then I notice a purchasing agent. How many things must be purchased for the department? Could not the services of the purchasing agent of the Department of Marine 'be obtained for the purchase of the things required for this department? Is it necessary that every little department should have a purchasing agent?
I notice that the last auditor general's report gives the salary of this man as $2,862, but he is now slated at $3,420.
Then we find what I think is the gem of the whole collection, a director of publicity.
What does the Department of Fisheries need with a director of publicity? What does he do? Before this item passes I intend to ask for full information on that. Then when I get it, I am going to ask what his assistant does. I have no doubt that if I looked further into this matter I would find that the assistant had an assistant, probably under the designation of clerk or something of that kind. Then we find a director of fisheries promotion and inspection. This gentleman receives a very substantial salary. Possibly he does useful work, but when the general services of this department are being reduced by $185,112, as will be found on page 44, I cannot understand why there should be an increase of $4,893 in the salaries of the permanent staff at Ottawa.
It is not possible to get full details for British Columbia as the auditor general's report is about two years old when it is issued, but I am sure the same conditions prevail there, i.f they are not worse. I believe they have a director of publicity, but he goes under a different name, something to do with statistics. I should like the minister to give me some explanation about these matters. First, what are the duties of the director of publicity and his assistant?

In reply to the hon. gentleman's direct question I may say that the director of publicity and his assistant collect statistics and distribute them throughout the country and the world in an effort to increase the demand for fish. The fisheries industry of Canada is worth about $34,000,000, the fisheries of the Pacific coast alone are estimated to be worth $20,000,000.
On page 77 I notice the salary for the private secretary shows an increase of $1,532.59. Why is that?

Last year there was not a private secretary engaged for the whole year. The estimates for next year provide for one being engaged for the full year.
Progress reported.
